claim: The woman who nourishes the unborn child must herself be nourished and protected.

cultivates.why: care for the one carrying the child is owed to her, as the child's own care
looking after the mother is the father's first act of parenting

needs: The verse speaks from the father's side: his own self has entered her as the embryo. Use only as a duty of care toward the mother, never as a statement about women.

commentary.reading: The wife nourishes the husband's self that has entered her as the embryo, so she who nourishes is to be nourished and protected by him; this is the first of a person's three births.
commentary.source: Shankara on Aitareya 2.1.2-3 (adhyaya 2)

claim: Wealth can give a comfortable life but cannot give immortality.

heals.why: even the whole earth's wealth only buys the life of the well-off; it cannot deliver what the wanting is really after
names the ceiling on what more money can do

cultivates.why: separates what wealth can do from what it cannot

needs: The scene: Yajnavalkya is leaving home and dividing his property. Not for someone in real money trouble, to whom it sounds dismissive.

commentary.reading: Wealth is only a means to rites and comforts; immortality cannot even be hoped for through wealth or the works it pays for. The dialogue grounds the turn to self-knowledge.
commentary.source: Shankara on Brihadaranyaka 2.4.2

claim: What cannot make me immortal is of no use to me; teach me what you know.

depicts.why: Maitreyi turns down what is offered and asks for the one thing that lasts
spoken by someone who sees that having everything would still leave the real question open

cultivates.why: models asking of any gain: will this give me what I actually want

needs: Reads best after 2.4.2 where the offer of property is made.

commentary.reading: Maitreyi, a brahmavadini, rejects wealth as useless for immortality and asks only for what Yajnavalkya knows as its means; he praises her for it.
commentary.source: Shankara on Brihadaranyaka 2.4.3

line_issue: 'Cannot save me' changes 'will not make me immortal' (amrita). Corrected: What would I do with something that cannot make me deathless? Tell me what you know instead.

claim: Wealth, honour and learning do not tell a person where he goes when he leaves this world.

depicts.why: a king who has everything admits plainly: I do not know

heals.why: success and study have not answered the one question that remains

needs: Must be followed by the answer (the self as one's own light, 4.3), or it only frightens.

commentary.reading: Janaka is equipped with meditations as a traveller with a chariot or boat, yet does not know his destination; Yajnavalkya then teaches the self and declares him to have reached fearlessness (4.2.4).
commentary.source: Shankara on Brihadaranyaka 4.2.1

claim: When every outer light and even speech has gone, the self is the light by which a person sits, moves and works.

heals.why: when every outside support has gone dark, there is still something in you that sees and by which you go on
even with no one's voice to follow, you are not left without light
the darkness described is total, and the verse still finds a light in it

cultivates.why: points to the awareness that remains when sun, moon, fire and speech are all gone

commentary.reading: The self is a light other than the body and organs, self-luminous; by it the person acts when no outer light remains, as is seen in dream.
commentary.source: Shankara on Brihadaranyaka 4.3.6

claim: A person is made of desire: desire shapes resolve, resolve shapes action, and action shapes what one becomes.

heals.why: shows where a want leads, step by step, before it has become a life

cultivates.why: lets a person trace what they are becoming back to what they keep wanting
if will follows desire, choosing what to want is where change starts

needs: In context this explains rebirth and bondage; the next verse praises the one free of desire. The motivational reading is partial.

commentary.reading: Desire is the root of transmigration: one's resolve and action follow desire, and one attains the result of that action. The desireless knower is treated next (4.4.6).
commentary.source: Shankara on Brihadaranyaka 4.4.5

claim: The self is to be known in this very life; not knowing it is the great loss.

heals.why: says the chance to know is now, while we are still here

cultivates.why: makes knowing oneself the thing not to postpone

commentary.reading: Being in this very body we have somehow known Brahman; had we not, the loss, endless birth and death, would have been great. Knowers become immortal, others go to sorrow.
commentary.source: Shankara on Brihadaranyaka 4.4.14

line_issue: The verse states 'we have known it', not 'let us know it'. Corrected: Here, in this very life, we have come to know it. Not to have known it would have been the great loss.

claim: Having known the self alone, cultivate insight and do not dwell on many words, which only weary speech.

heals.why: permission to stop multiplying words and arguments and stay with one thing

cultivates.why: fewer words, one object of attention
keeps to the one thing worth knowing

needs: Addressed to a seeker of the self; applying it to ordinary overthinking is an extension.

commentary.reading: After knowing the self from teacher and scripture, the seeker should practise the means of insight; many words are to be dropped since they only tire the organ of speech.
commentary.source: Shankara on Brihadaranyaka 4.4.21

line_issue: 'That only tires you' loosens 'weariness of speech'. Acceptable; a closer line: Know the one, and let insight grow from it. Do not dwell on many words; they only wear out the voice.

claim: The one syllable Da teaches three duties: self-control, giving and compassion.

heals.why: to humans, who hold on, the syllable says give
to the cruel streak, the syllable says be compassionate

cultivates.why: dayadhvam: be compassionate
datta: give according to your means

commentary.reading: Gods lack restraint, humans are greedy, asuras are cruel; all three are found among humans, so a person should learn all three: restraint, giving, compassion.
commentary.source: Shankara on Brihadaranyaka 5.2.1-3

claim: A prayer to be led from the unreal to the real, from darkness to light, from death to immortality.

depicts.why: the voice of someone who wants what is real and asks to be led to it

cultivates.why: asking to be led is itself an act of trust
the prayer does not claim to find the way alone

commentary.reading: The unreal and darkness both mean death, that is, natural ignorant thought and action; the real and light mean immortality, one's divine nature. The third line sums up the first two. A japa for the chanter.
commentary.source: Shankara on Brihadaranyaka 1.3.28

claim: Nothing is higher than dharma; through it the weak can stand up to the strong, and dharma is truth.

heals.why: being in the right is a real power when facing someone stronger
the wronged person is told their ground is the highest there is
the weaker party is not without standing

cultivates.why: stand on what is true and right, as one would stand behind a king

commentary.reading: Dharma rules even the ruler; so even a weaker man hopes to overcome a stronger one through dharma, as through the king. Dharma in practice and truth as known from scripture are one.
commentary.source: Shankara on Brihadaranyaka 1.4.14

claim: All this is Brahman; a person is made of resolve and becomes what he resolves, so one should form a resolve.

cultivates.why: what you settle your conviction on is what you become
the verse asks for the meditation to be done calm, seeing all this as one

needs: The resolve meant is a settled conviction in meditation on Brahman as one's own self (3.14.2-4), not any life goal.

commentary.reading: Kratu is firm conviction. As a person's conviction is here, so he becomes after departing; therefore one should form the conviction taught next, the self within the heart.
commentary.source: Shankara on Chandogya 3.14.1

line_issue: The line drops 'All this is Brahman' and turns a meditative conviction into goal-setting. Corrected: All this is Brahman. A person is made of what he holds to; as he holds to it here, so he becomes. So choose what you hold to.

claim: A mother tells her son plainly that she does not know his lineage and that he should say exactly that.

heals.why: an origin one cannot account for is stated plainly, without apology
she gives him a name that is enough to stand on: Satyakama, son of Jabala

cultivates.why: truth about oneself said without shame

needs: Tell the whole Satyakama story. Do not speculate about the mother's past.

commentary.reading: Jabala says she was busy serving guests in her husband's house and never asked the gotra; she had him in her youth and his father then died. The tradition does not read unknown paternity here.
commentary.source: Shankara on Chandogya 4.4.2

claim: The teacher accepts the boy because he did not swerve from the truth about himself.

heals.why: the fact he feared would shut him out is what opens the door
worth is read from truthfulness

cultivates.why: honesty about oneself is honoured as nobility

commentary.reading: Gautama infers the boy's brahminhood from his truthfulness: none but a brahmin would speak so straight. He initiates him for not departing from truth.
commentary.source: Shankara on Chandogya 4.4.5

line_issue: The line replaces 'brahmin' with 'truly noble'. A gloss, not the text. Closer: 'No one but a true brahmin could speak so plainly. You have not left the truth. I will teach you.'

claim: Given four hundred weak cows, Satyakama vowed not to return until they were a thousand and stayed away for years.

cultivates.why: he sets his own measure for the task and names it aloud
years of quiet work on an unpromising start

commentary.reading: Understanding the teacher's intent, he took the lean cows to a forest and vowed not to return short of a thousand; his faith and austerity are what later bring him the teaching.
commentary.source: Shankara on Chandogya 4.4.5

claim: A father asks his conceited, learned son whether he asked for the teaching by which the unknown becomes known.

heals.why: twelve years of learning are shown to have missed the one thing
pride in knowledge is met with a question it cannot answer

cultivates.why: the son ends by asking: how could there be such a teaching

commentary.reading: Seeing his son proud and stiff, unlike one who has the real teaching, the father asks about the instruction on the one Being by knowing which all is known.
commentary.source: Shankara on Chandogya 6.1.2-3

claim: The mind flies in every direction, finds no resting place elsewhere, and settles on that to which it is tied.

depicts.why: a tethered bird flying every way and finding no perch

heals.why: the restless mind is not broken; it has a home it returns to
the flying about ends in rest, every night

cultivates.why: rest is where the mind is already tied

commentary.reading: Prana here means Being (sat), the supreme self: the mind, wearied by waking and dream, rests in it in deep sleep as the bird returns to its post.
commentary.source: Shankara on Chandogya 6.8.2

line_issue: Shankara reads 'prana' here as Being, the self, not the physical breath, so 'returns to the breath' is literal but narrower than the tradition. Safer: Like a bird on a string, the mind flies everywhere, finds no rest, and comes back to the life it is tied to.

claim: The subtle essence that is the self of all this is the truth and the self, and you are that.

heals.why: what you are at root is what everything is at root; smallness does not reach it
the self the verse points to is not the one that failed
an empty person is told they are made of the one thing that is real

cultivates.why: the plainest statement of identity in the Upanishads

commentary.reading: 'That' is Being, the root and self of all; 'you' is Shvetaketu freed of identification with body and mind. The sentence states their identity, repeated nine times.
commentary.source: Shankara on Chandogya 6.8.7

claim: The body dies when the living self leaves it; the living self does not die.

heals.why: what died is the body; the one who lived in it is not said to have died
death is located in the body, away from the one who lives

cultivates.why: the tree lesson: life withdraws from a branch and the branch dries, but life is not what dried

needs: The reader must accept a self distinct from the body. Not for the first raw days of a loss.

commentary.reading: Bereft of the jiva the body dies; the jiva does not die, as its continuing after sleep and its carrying results of action show. That subtle essence is the self.
commentary.source: Shankara on Chandogya 6.11.3

line_issue: 'Life itself' blurs jiva, the living self. Corrected: The body dies when the living self leaves it. The living self does not die.

claim: The great banyan stands from a subtle essence in the seed that the eye cannot see; so have faith.

heals.why: not seeing something is shown to be no proof that nothing is there

cultivates.why: the father asks for trust exactly where the eye gives out

commentary.reading: The gross world arises from subtle Being that is not perceived, as the banyan from the unseen essence of the seed; faith is asked because the subtle is hard to hold even when reasoned.
commentary.source: Shankara on Chandogya 6.12.1-2

line_issue: 'From that unseen nothing' contradicts the chapter, which denies that being comes from nothing. Corrected: Break a banyan seed and you see nothing. From that fine essence you cannot see, the great tree stands. Have faith.

claim: Like salt dissolved in water, the real is present everywhere here though it cannot be seen.

heals.why: absence to the eye and presence in every sip can both be true
what cannot be seen is said to be right here, always

cultivates.why: learn to know by another means what the eye misses
Being pervades this very body as salt pervades the water

commentary.reading: Being, the root of the world, is in this very body though the senses do not find it, as dissolved salt is known by taste and not by touch or sight.
commentary.source: Shankara on Chandogya 6.13.1-2

claim: As a blindfolded man gets home once someone frees his eyes and points the way, one with a teacher comes to know.

depicts.why: brought here blindfolded and left, turning every way and calling out

heals.why: being lost is a blindfold that can be untied, and the way home can be asked for
there is a home and it can be reached village by village

cultivates.why: accepting direction from one who knows the way

commentary.reading: The blindfold is delusion and desire; the compassionate teacher removes it and points to one's own self, Being. One who has a teacher knows; his delay lasts only until the body falls.
commentary.source: Shankara on Chandogya 6.14.1-2

claim: One who knows many texts but not the self remains in sorrow; the knower of the self crosses sorrow.

depicts.why: 'I am in sorrow, sir', said by the most learned man of his age
everything has been studied and it has not filled him
he asks to be taken across

commentary.reading: Narada's sorrow is that of one who has not reached his end in spite of all learning; all he has studied is name only. The knower of the self goes beyond sorrow.
commentary.source: Shankara on Chandogya 7.1.3

claim: Steadfastness comes only through doing; no one becomes steadfast without acting.

heals.why: waiting to feel steady before acting is the wrong order
steadiness is the result of acting, so doubt is not settled by more thought

cultivates.why: steadiness is built by the doing itself
act first; firmness follows

commentary.reading: Kriti, doing, is here the restraint of the senses and concentration of the mind; only with it does steadfast devotion to the teacher and the truth arise.
commentary.source: Shankara on Chandogya 7.21.1

claim: The infinite alone is happiness; there is no happiness in the small.

heals.why: the small always leaves a thirst for more; the wanting is for the vast
emptiness after getting the small things is what the verse predicts
more of the finite is still finite

cultivates.why: points happiness to what has no edge
the infinite is later shown to be the self (7.25)

commentary.reading: The finite breeds thirst for more, and thirst is the seed of sorrow; so there is no happiness in the small. Only the infinite, which leaves nothing further to want, is happiness.
commentary.source: Shankara on Chandogya 7.23.1

claim: Like people walking over buried gold, all beings enter the world of Brahman daily in sleep and do not find it.

heals.why: the sense that nothing is here is answered: the treasure is under your own feet
no one is poorer in this than anyone else; everyone carries the same gold

cultivates.why: the self in the heart is visited nightly; it only goes unrecognised
makes one want to learn the spot

commentary.reading: Creatures reach the Brahman-world, the self in the space of the heart, daily in deep sleep, yet do not know it because they are drawn away by untruth, that is, by desire and ignorance.
commentary.source: Shankara on Chandogya 8.3.2 (dahara vidya; not Prajapati's teaching, which begins at 8.7)

claim: All that moves in this world is pervaded by the Lord; live by renouncing and do not covet anyone's wealth.

heals.why: if everything is the Lord's, there is nothing to grab
'whose wealth is it?' takes the sting out of what others have

cultivates.why: enjoying what is given without the grip of ownership
holding lightly is made the way to enjoy
what you have is seen as held in trust

needs: Not for someone in real money stress; it is about how one holds what one has.

commentary.reading: Shankara: all this is to be covered by the Lord, the self; 'tena tyaktena bhunjithah' means protect the self by that renunciation, addressed to the knower who gives up desires. Gita Press and most later teachers read: enjoy what is given, with detachment.
commentary.source: Shankara on Isha 1; Gita Press Ishadi Nau Upanishad

claim: One should wish to live a hundred years doing one's work; for such a person action does not cling.

heals.why: the verse wants you to want a full life, and gives work as the way to live it

cultivates.why: wish for the whole hundred years, doing what is yours to do
a lifelong, steady way of working

commentary.reading: For one who cannot yet take to knowledge with renunciation and wishes to live, there is no way other than doing the enjoined works, so that evil action does not cling.
commentary.source: Shankara on Isha 2

claim: One who sees all beings in the self and the self in all beings does not recoil from anyone.

heals.why: revulsion needs an 'other'; the verse removes the other
no being is outside the one self, so no one is finally a stranger
there is no second person to measure against

cultivates.why: goodwill follows from seeing one's own self in each person
the self is shown as what is shared by all beings

needs: Never as advice to someone being mistreated to stop objecting.

commentary.reading: Revulsion arises on seeing something bad as other than oneself. For one who sees the pure self everywhere without a break, there is no object of revulsion.
commentary.source: Shankara on Isha 6

line_issue: The verse describes a seer; the line turns it into an instruction. Corrected: One who sees all beings in the self, and the self in all beings, no longer recoils from anyone.

claim: The good and the pleasant both come to a person; the wise choose the good, the dull choose the pleasant.

heals.why: a hard choice gets one clear question: which of these is the good and which only pleasant
names the pull of the pleasant as a choice, not a fate
drifting toward the easy option is shown to be a decision

cultivates.why: examine the two closely and tell them apart

needs: 'The dull' and 'the foolish' can sting someone already ashamed of a choice.

commentary.reading: Shreyas is the good that leads to freedom, preyas the pleasant; they come mixed. The wise separate them as a swan separates milk from water; the short-sighted choose the pleasant for the body's getting and keeping.
commentary.source: Shankara on Katha 1.2.2

claim: Arise, awake, go to the great teachers and learn; the path is sharp and hard to cross like a razor's edge.

heals.why: a direct call out of drift
arise, awake

cultivates.why: the call is to get up now
go to those who know and learn
it is honest that the path is hard, which makes the resolve real

needs: Too loud for an exhausted or collapsed reader.

commentary.reading: Arise: turn toward knowledge of the self. Awake: end the sleep of ignorance. Approach excellent teachers and understand the self they teach. The path of knowledge is as hard to walk as a razor's edge.
commentary.source: Shankara on Katha 1.3.14

claim: The self is the rider, the body the chariot, the intellect the charioteer, the mind the reins and the senses the horses.

heals.why: a runaway mind is horses without a hand on the reins; it can be driven

cultivates.why: judgement is given the driver's seat over impulse
you are the one carried, not the vehicle or the horses

commentary.reading: The self joined with body, senses and mind is the experiencer, the master of the chariot; the intellect drives, the mind as reins holds the senses, which run among their objects.
commentary.source: Shankara on Katha 1.3.3-4

claim: The senses face outward, so people look out; a rare wise one turns the gaze inward and sees the self.

heals.why: the outward pull is how the senses are built, not a private failing
if nothing out there has satisfied, the verse says where no one has yet looked

cultivates.why: the self is found by turning the gaze around
invites being the rare one who looks in

commentary.reading: The Lord made the senses outgoing, so people see outer things and not the inner self. A rare discerning person, wanting immortality, turns them back as one turns a river and sees the inner self.
commentary.source: Shankara on Katha 2.1.1

claim: Do not torment the body over pleasure and pain; do not gloat when praised or curse others when blamed.

heals.why: blame does not have to be answered with a curse
praise does not have to be swallowed

cultivates.why: the same face for praise and blame
hold back the harsh word when criticised

needs: A rule from a renunciant's code; offer it as conduct under criticism, never to someone who has been wronged.

commentary.reading: Among the rules for a sannyasin: no excess strain on the body for pleasure or pain, no elation at praise, no cursing when reviled.
commentary.source: Katharudra (Kanthashruti) Upanishad, a Sannyasa Upanishad; plain sense, no bhashya checked

claim: Without attention behind them, speech and the senses convey nothing; one says, my mind was elsewhere.

depicts.why: 'my mind was elsewhere, I did not catch that' is said in the reader's own voice

heals.why: shows that being present is what lets anything in at all
locates the loss in where attention was, which can be changed

commentary.reading: Indra teaches that no sense makes anything known apart from prajna, conscious intelligence. The Brahma Sutra (1.1.28-31, with Shankara) takes the prana and prajna of this chapter as Brahman.
commentary.source: Kaushitaki 3.7 plain sense; Shankara on Brahma Sutra 1.1.28-31 for the chapter

claim: A father admits to his son that he too does not know and proposes that they both go and learn.

heals.why: an elder says 'I do not know' without loss of standing
not knowing is treated as a reason to go and ask, nothing more

cultivates.why: father and son become students together

commentary.reading: King Chitra Gangyayani asks Shvetaketu a question he cannot answer; his father Uddalaka admits the same and both go to the king as students, fuel in hand.
commentary.source: Kaushitaki 1.1 plain sense; no bhashya checked

claim: Misfortune, mental distress and craving all come from ego; there is no greater enemy than ego.

heals.why: traces three kinds of trouble back to the one sense of 'I'

cultivates.why: look for the 'I' behind the upset

needs: Nidagha is speaking of his own ego. Turned on a reader in pain it becomes blame.

commentary.reading: Part of Nidagha's dispassionate lament before his teacher: ego is the root of calamity, anguish and wanting.
commentary.source: Maha Upanishad, Ribhu and Nidagha dialogue; plain sense. The verse parallels the Yoga Vasishtha; no classical bhashya checked (Vairagya Prakarana)

claim: The mind runs here and there, restless and to no purpose, wandering far like a dog in a village.

depicts.why: a seeker describes his own mind running everywhere for nothing

commentary.reading: Nidagha describes his own mind to his teacher before asking for the way out.
commentary.source: Maha Upanishad, Ribhu and Nidagha dialogue; plain sense. The verse parallels the Yoga Vasishtha; no classical bhashya checked (Vairagya Prakarana)

claim: Mastering the mind is harder than drinking the ocean, uprooting Mount Meru or swallowing fire.

depicts.why: the speaker has tried and found his mind harder than any feat

heals.why: failing to control the mind is the common human case, not a personal weakness

needs: Follow with a verse that gives a way in (4.2-3), or it reads as hopeless.

commentary.reading: Nidagha's lament on the difficulty of restraining the mind; the answer comes in Ribhu's teaching on calm and inquiry.
commentary.source: Maha Upanishad, Ribhu and Nidagha dialogue; plain sense. The verse parallels the Yoga Vasishtha; no classical bhashya checked (Vairagya Prakarana)

claim: Misfortune, good fortune, birth and death each come in a moment; all of it is perishable.

heals.why: good fortune is as momentary as bad
nothing here was ever going to stay

cultivates.why: sees gain and loss as equally brief
the same clock runs on good and bad times

commentary.reading: Spoken in dispassion: everything in the world, fortune and misfortune, birth and death, is momentary and perishable. It is a lament, not a comfort that things will improve.
commentary.source: Maha Upanishad, Ribhu and Nidagha dialogue; plain sense. The verse parallels the Yoga Vasishtha; no classical bhashya checked (Vairagya Prakarana)

line_issue: The line drops birth and death and softens 'perishable' into 'passes'. Corrected: Hard times come in a moment and good times come in a moment. Birth, then death, in a moment. None of it lasts.

claim: Calm, inquiry, contentment and good company guard the door of freedom; win one fully and the other three follow.

heals.why: the task is cut down to one thing to hold
you need only begin with one of four

cultivates.why: calm is the first gatekeeper
contentment is named as a door, not a reward
inquiry is one of the four

commentary.reading: Shama, vichara, santosha and sadhu-sangama are the four doorkeepers of moksha; serving even one with full effort brings the rest.
commentary.source: Maha Upanishad, Ribhu and Nidagha dialogue; plain sense. The verse parallels the Yoga Vasishtha; no classical bhashya checked (Mumukshu Prakarana)

claim: All sorrows, craving and unbearable anxieties vanish in calm minds, as darkness vanishes before the sun.

heals.why: anxiety is said to end where the mind becomes calm
craving is included in what calm dissolves

cultivates.why: gives a reason to value calm above fixing each worry

needs: Gives no method. To an anxious reader alone it can sound like 'just be calm'; pair with a practice.

commentary.reading: In praise of shama, the first doorkeeper: for those whose minds are calm, all sorrows and cravings perish.
commentary.source: Maha Upanishad, Ribhu and Nidagha dialogue; plain sense. The verse parallels the Yoga Vasishtha; no classical bhashya checked (Mumukshu Prakarana)

claim: No elixir and no wealth gives the happiness that inner calm gives.

heals.why: what fortune is chased for is said to come more surely from calm
the thing envied in others is not where happiness is

cultivates.why: ranks calm above every outer gain
happiness is placed within reach, inside

commentary.reading: In praise of shama: neither the elixir of life nor the embrace of Lakshmi gives the happiness of inner calm.
commentary.source: Maha Upanishad, Ribhu and Nidagha dialogue; plain sense. The verse parallels the Yoga Vasishtha; no classical bhashya checked (Mumukshu Prakarana)

claim: Restlessness is the nature of the mind, as heat is the nature of fire; no mind is without it.

heals.why: a restless mind is doing what minds do; it is no defect of character
naming it as nature takes away the fight with it

commentary.reading: Movement is the mind's own property; the teaching goes on to say that the mind stilled by knowledge is freedom.
commentary.source: Maha Upanishad, Ribhu and Nidagha dialogue; plain sense. The verse parallels the Yoga Vasishtha; no classical bhashya checked

claim: Your own mind is the boat across craving; cut the mind's noose with the mind, for no one else can lift you.

heals.why: stops the wait for someone else to do it
the mind that is caught is also the tool that frees

cultivates.why: self-reliance: the means is already yours
lift yourself across

needs: 'No one else can carry you' is wrong for a lonely or collapsed reader and sits against a devotional plan.

commentary.reading: Self-effort is the means: the mind binds and the mind, used rightly, releases. Compare Gita 6.5, raise yourself by yourself.
commentary.source: Maha Upanishad, Ribhu and Nidagha dialogue; plain sense. The verse parallels the Yoga Vasishtha; no classical bhashya checked

line_issue: The line drops the boat image and 'craving'. Fuller: When craving has you in its jaws, your own mind is the boat. Cut the mind's knot with the mind and lift yourself across; no one else can carry you.

claim: One who takes up full effort and acts by sound guidance without anxiety is sure to succeed.

heals.why: fear of failing is met with a plain list of what makes success likely
effort is named as the deciding thing

cultivates.why: full effort, steadily
backs the decision to begin and keep going

needs: Not after a failure, when 'who would not succeed' reads as blame.

commentary.reading: Human effort (paurusha) carried out as the shastra directs and without agitation does not fail.
commentary.source: Maha Upanishad, Ribhu and Nidagha dialogue; plain sense. The verse parallels the Yoga Vasishtha; no classical bhashya checked (the paurusha teaching). The Sanskrit in the record has copy errors

claim: In worldly dealings, let go of what is lost and take up what comes.

heals.why: a lost deal, job or plan is allowed to be over
attention is turned to what has actually arrived

cultivates.why: no second look at what has gone
loss and gain get the same light hand

needs: About gains and losses in dealings, not about people one has lost or wrongs one has suffered.

commentary.reading: Addressed to Nidagha as a knower of truth: in the transactions of worldly life, disregard what is lost and accept what comes.
commentary.source: Maha Upanishad, Ribhu and Nidagha dialogue; plain sense. The verse parallels the Yoga Vasishtha; no classical bhashya checked

line_issue: Dropping 'in worldly dealings' lets it be read about bereavement. Corrected: In the give and take of life, let what is lost go, and take up what comes.

claim: As husk leaves rice and tarnish leaves copper through work, a person's inborn impurity surely goes through effort; so be industrious.

heals.why: the flaw is husk on the grain, not the grain
even a fault you were born with is said to go, without doubt

cultivates.why: so keep working
effort is promised a result

commentary.reading: A person's impurity, though natural like the husk of rice, is removed by action; therefore one should be industrious.
commentary.source: Maha Upanishad, Ribhu and Nidagha dialogue; plain sense. The verse parallels the Yoga Vasishtha; no classical bhashya checked

claim: One who does the work that comes, sees friend and foe alike and speaks gently does not sink in worldly life.

heals.why: doing the work that has come leaves less room for dread

cultivates.why: the same regard for friend and opponent
speaks what is agreeable and gently, and understands what others intend
neither grieving nor craving

needs: A portrait of a free person, not a demand to be pleasant to someone who is mistreating you.

commentary.reading: Marks of the one liberated while living, who acts in the world without sinking in it.
commentary.source: Maha Upanishad, Ribhu and Nidagha dialogue; plain sense. The verse parallels the Yoga Vasishtha; no classical bhashya checked

claim: Be outwardly active and inwardly unagitated, a doer outside and a non-doer within, moving through the world with a clear mind.

heals.why: the strain is located in inner agitation, which can be set down while the work goes on
effort outside, stillness inside

cultivates.why: act fully without the inner heat
a non-doer within

commentary.reading: The free person shows energy outwardly as the occasion needs, with none of its agitation in the heart: a doer outside, a non-doer within.
commentary.source: Maha Upanishad, Ribhu and Nidagha dialogue; plain sense. The verse parallels the Yoga Vasishtha; no classical bhashya checked

claim: Counting people as one's own or not is small-minded; for the generous-hearted the whole earth is family.

heals.why: the line between ours and theirs is shown as a habit of counting
an outsider anywhere is still inside the one family

cultivates.why: kinship is extended to everyone on earth
a large heart is defined by whom it includes

needs: Not as a reply to someone whose family is treating them badly.

commentary.reading: A mark of the liberated: the reckoning of 'mine' and 'not mine' belongs to narrow minds; the noble treat the earth as one household.
commentary.source: Maha Upanishad, Ribhu and Nidagha dialogue; plain sense. The verse parallels the Yoga Vasishtha; no classical bhashya checked

claim: The mind itself is samsara, so purify it with effort; what one's mind dwells on, that one becomes.

heals.why: the weight is traced to where the mind keeps dwelling, which can be changed
the round one feels trapped in is located in the mind, not the world

cultivates.why: watch what the mind rests on, because one takes its shape
cleaning the mind is named as work worth effort

commentary.reading: The round of bondage is nothing but the mind; one becomes of the nature of what the mind holds. Hence the mind is to be purified with effort.
commentary.source: Maitri (Maitrayaniya) Upanishad 6.34; plain sense, Ramatirtha's dipika not checked

line_issue: 'Your world' softens samsara, the round of bondage. Closer: The mind itself is the round we are caught in; clean it with care. What your mind dwells on, you become.

claim: If the mind were as attached to Brahman as it is to sense objects, anyone would be freed from bondage.

heals.why: the power to cling is not condemned; it is only pointed the wrong way
the same grip, turned to the highest, frees

cultivates.why: one already has the strength of attachment the path needs

commentary.reading: The mind's fixedness on objects, if given to Brahman, would release anyone.
commentary.source: Maitri Upanishad 6.34; plain sense

claim: The mind alone causes bondage and liberation: attached to objects it binds, free of objects it liberates.

heals.why: binding is put in the hook, not in the things
what holds you is inside and so within reach

cultivates.why: see which way the mind is facing
freedom is defined as the mind unhooked

commentary.reading: The mind is the single cause of both bondage and release, by attachment to objects or freedom from them. The verse recurs in Amritabindu Upanishad 2.
commentary.source: Maitri Upanishad 6.34; plain sense

claim: The body is a temple and the living being in it is Shiva alone; discard ignorance and worship as 'I am He'.

heals.why: the one who lives in this body is named as Shiva himself
what is to be thrown out is ignorance, like stale flowers, not oneself

cultivates.why: worship is to be done as identity: I am He
the body is given the dignity of a shrine

commentary.reading: The body is the temple, the jiva is Shiva alone; ignorance is the withered offering to be removed, and the worship is the awareness 'I am He'.
commentary.source: Maitreya Upanishad 2.1 (the verse also appears in Skanda Upanishad); plain sense, no bhashya checked

line_issue: 'The life within it is divine' softens 'the jiva is Shiva alone' and drops the worship. Corrected: Your body is a temple, and the one who lives in it is Shiva himself. Clear out ignorance like yesterday's flowers, and worship knowing 'I am He'.

claim: There are two kinds of knowledge: the lower, the Vedas and their sciences, and the higher, by which the imperishable is reached.

heals.why: learning that has not satisfied is explained: it was one kind of knowing, and there is another
all scholarship, even scripture, is ranked as the lower knowledge

cultivates.why: opens the question of what the higher knowing is
tells information apart from knowing what does not perish

commentary.reading: The lower knowledge covers dharma and its results, even the Vedas as text; the higher is the direct knowing of the imperishable, not merely the words of the Upanishads.
commentary.source: Shankara on Mundaka 1.1.4-5

claim: Seeing that the unmade cannot be won by action, a seeker should turn dispassionate and go to a teacher established in Brahman.

depicts.why: the verse names the moment of having looked at everything work can win and finding it not enough

heals.why: disenchantment after achievement is treated as the right starting point, not a breakdown

cultivates.why: what is made by effort ends; what is unmade is not got by more effort
go and ask someone who knows

needs: In Shankara this qualifies a person for renunciation. Offer it as a turn toward inquiry, not as a reason to quit work or family.

commentary.reading: Having examined all worlds gained by action and seen them as impermanent, the brahmana comes to dispassion: the uncreated is not attained by the created. He should go, fuel in hand, only to a teacher both learned and established in Brahman.
commentary.source: Shankara on Mundaka 1.2.12

claim: Two companion birds cling to one tree; one eats the sweet fruit, the other looks on without eating.

heals.why: beside the one who tastes every result there is one who only watches and is not shaken
there is a seat in you that does not move with the eating
the next verse says the first bird stops grieving when it sees the other

cultivates.why: the witness is shown as one's closest companion on the same tree
watching without eating

needs: Reads fully with 3.1.2: sunk and grieving, the one sees the other and is freed from sorrow.

commentary.reading: One bird is the individual self tasting the fruits of action, pleasant and painful; the other is the Lord, the ever-free witness, who only looks on.
commentary.source: Shankara on Mundaka 3.1.1

claim: Truth alone prevails, not falsehood; by truth is laid the path the sages walk to the highest abode of truth.

heals.why: the one who was lied to is told that falsehood does not have the last word
telling the truth is the side that prevails
when the honest option is costly, it is still the road that goes somewhere

cultivates.why: stand on what is true
truth wins over time, so one can hold

needs: Truth prevails in the long run; no promise of a quick result.

commentary.reading: It is the truthful one who wins, not the liar; the path of the gods is spread out by truth, and sages free of deceit and desire go by it.
commentary.source: Shankara on Mundaka 3.1.6

claim: Caste belongs to no part of the body and not to the self; it is a convention made for worldly dealings.

heals.why: a label fixed at birth is denied any hold on what one is
shame about origin has nothing in the self to attach to

cultivates.why: one's standing rests on the self, which has no rank

commentary.reading: In a list of definitions: jati is not of skin, blood, flesh or bone, nor of the self; it is fashioned for vyavahara, practical dealings.
commentary.source: Niralamba Upanishad 10; plain sense, no bhashya checked

claim: Sukesha told the prince plainly that he did not know, for one who speaks untruth dries up to the root.

heals.why: the fear of being found not to know is met by simply saying so, even to a prince
'I do not know' is shown as the honourable answer

cultivates.why: he let the prince leave unimpressed and kept his word clean

commentary.reading: One who speaks falsehood perishes root and all, losing this world and the next; so Sukesha would not lie. The story shows how hard this knowledge is to get and the truthfulness it needs.
commentary.source: Shankara on Prashna 6.1

claim: The joy of a learned person untouched by desire equals each order of joy above the fullest human happiness.

heals.why: the whole earth's wealth is only the first rung of the scale
the one envied, young, strong and rich, holds one unit

cultivates.why: joy grows as wanting falls
freedom from desire is counted as joy, not loss

commentary.reading: Joy multiplies a hundredfold at each step as desire thins; the learned one not struck by desire has each of those joys, up to the bliss of Brahman.
commentary.source: Shankara on Taittiriya 2.8

claim: The knower of the bliss of Brahman is no longer tormented by thoughts of good left undone or wrong done.

depicts.why: 'why did I not do good, why did I do wrong' is quoted in the tormented person's own words

heals.why: there is a ground in oneself where this self-torment does not burn

cultivates.why: the same passage says the knower fears nothing from anywhere
the self is known as joy, beyond the ledger of deeds

needs: Said of one who knows the self. It ends self-torment; it does not cancel the need to make amends.

commentary.reading: Regret over merit omitted and sin committed, which burns people as death nears, does not burn the knower, who sees both as the self.
commentary.source: Shankara on Taittiriya 2.9

claim: Joy is Brahman: from joy beings are born, by joy they live, and into joy they return.

heals.why: existence is said to rest on joy from start to end, however flat it feels now

cultivates.why: joy is named as the source one comes from and lives by
being alive at all is seen as living by joy
Bhrigu's last finding: the deepest layer of oneself is joy

needs: The last clause speaks of beings departing into joy; keep the line's wording and do not use it as comfort about someone's dying.

commentary.reading: After food, breath, mind and understanding, Bhrigu knows bliss as Brahman, the innermost self, from which beings arise, by which they live and into which they merge.
commentary.source: Shankara on Taittiriya 3.6

claim: Speak the truth, practise dharma, and do not neglect your study.

cultivates.why: three plain commitments to carry into working life
study is to be kept up, not finished

commentary.reading: After teaching the Veda the teacher instructs in conduct: speak what is known to be true, do what is enjoined, and never be careless about recitation and study.
commentary.source: Shankara on Taittiriya 1.11.1

claim: Do not neglect duties to gods and ancestors; regard mother, father, teacher and guest as divine.

cultivates.why: those who raised and taught you are to be honoured as one honours a deity
the guest and the elder are served as sacred

needs: Honouring parents never means accepting mistreatment.

commentary.reading: Mother, father, teacher and guest are to be worshipped as deities; duties to gods and ancestors are not to be skipped.
commentary.source: Shankara on Taittiriya 1.11.2

claim: Give with faith, in plenty, with modesty, with awe and with understanding; do not give without faith.

heals.why: giving is taught as part of an educated life
give with modesty, so the gift does not feed the giver's pride

cultivates.why: how to give is spelled out in six ways
give with understanding of the one who receives

commentary.reading: Gifts are to be given with faith, according to one's prosperity, with modesty, with fear, and with friendliness or understanding.
commentary.source: Shankara on Taittiriya 1.11.3

line_issue: 'Bhiya deyam' is 'give with awe (fear)', not 'respect'. Corrected: Give with faith, never without it. Give generously, give modestly, give with awe, give with understanding.

claim: When in doubt about an action or conduct, act as thoughtful, gentle, dharma-loving people there would act.

heals.why: doubt gets a usable test: what would the fair and gentle people I know do here
when the rules run out there is still a way to decide

cultivates.why: judgement is borrowed from people who are thoughtful, unforced and not harsh

commentary.reading: In doubt about rites or conduct, follow the brahmanas of that place who are deliberate, practised, not directed by others, not cruel and desirous of dharma; likewise toward the accused.
commentary.source: Shankara on Taittiriya 1.11.3-4

claim: As moss pushed aside closes back at once, maya covers again even a wise person who turns away.

heals.why: explains why clarity slips the moment attention does

cultivates.why: practice has to be kept up, not done once

commentary.reading: Heedlessness toward the self lets ignorance cover even the learned again, as parted moss closes over water. The same verse stands in the Vivekachudamani on pramada.
commentary.source: Adhyatma Upanishad 15; parallel in Vivekachudamani (attributed to Shankara)

claim: One who stays even whether honoured by the good or tormented by the wicked is called liberated while living.

heals.why: the cruel do not get to set one's inner weather

cultivates.why: the same inner state under honour and under harassment

needs: A mark of a liberated person, not an instruction to stay where one is being harmed.

commentary.reading: One of the marks of the jivanmukta: evenness whether worshipped by the good or afflicted by the wicked.
commentary.source: Adhyatma Upanishad 47; parallel in Vivekachudamani

claim: Action begun before knowledge is not destroyed by knowledge and yields its fruit, like an arrow already released.

cultivates.why: consequences already in motion are met without surprise
one bears what was set going earlier

needs: The prarabdha teaching for a knower. Never as an explanation of someone's illness, loss or mistreatment.

commentary.reading: Prarabdha, action that has begun to bear fruit, continues for the knower until spent, as an arrow shot at a supposed tiger still strikes when the target is seen to be a cow.
commentary.source: Adhyatma Upanishad 53-54; parallel in Vivekachudamani

claim: A father who cares for his child from birth is caring for his own self and for the continuity of the worlds.

heals.why: the daily care of a child is given a meaning larger than the tiredness

cultivates.why: raising the child is counted as tending one's own self
the child is not other than oneself

commentary.reading: The son is the father's own self; in nourishing the child before and after birth he nourishes himself, so that the worlds continue. The child's birth is the father's second birth.
commentary.source: Shankara on Aitareya 2.1.3

line_issue: In the text the child's birth is the father's second birth. Closer: Caring for your child, you care for your own self; the child's birth is your second birth.

claim: The child takes the parent's place for good works; the parent, duties done and old, departs and is born again.

heals.why: a parent's passing is described as leaving with the work complete and carried on

cultivates.why: the child stands in the parent's place for what is good

needs: Assumes rebirth. For someone looking back on a parent's full life, not for a parent still ill.

commentary.reading: The son is set in the father's place to perform meritorious works; the father, his duties done and advanced in age, departs and is reborn. That is his third birth.
commentary.source: Shankara on Aitareya 2.1.4

claim: A husband, wife or child is dear not for their own sake but for the sake of the self.

heals.why: what one loves in every loved person is traced to the self, which is not lost with them

cultivates.why: the self is shown as what is dearest, and so what must be seen and known
the hold of each relationship is loosened by seeing what it rests on

needs: Shankara reads this as teaching dispassion toward family so that the self is sought. Easily heard as 'love is selfish'; not for a marriage in conflict or a fresh loss.

commentary.reading: To produce dispassion toward husband, wife and sons as a means to immortality: all are dear for the sake of one's own self, so the self alone is dear in the primary sense and is to be seen, heard of and reflected on.
commentary.source: Shankara on Brihadaranyaka 2.4.5

line_issue: The line is fair. The record's misuse note ('we love the one self shining in the other') is a modern gloss; Shankara reads it as: others are dear for one's own self's sake, so know the self.

claim: Desire for sons, wealth and worlds is one desire; the knower, done with learning, should live by the strength of knowing.

heals.why: family, money and standing are shown as one wanting in three forms
seeing the one desire behind the many loosens each

cultivates.why: the knower rises above all three

needs: The passage is the classic text for renunciation: knowers give up these desires and live on alms.

commentary.reading: Knowing the self, brahmanas renounce the desire for sons, wealth and worlds and live as mendicants. 'Balya' is the strength that comes of knowledge, living without other supports; then reflection (mauna), then one is a knower of Brahman.
commentary.source: Shankara on Brihadaranyaka 3.5.1

line_issue: 'Live with a child's simplicity' follows the literal 'balya'; Shankara reads it as the strength of self-knowledge, and the passage is about renouncing all three desires. Closer: Wanting children, wanting wealth, wanting standing are one wanting. Having learned, stand on what you know.

claim: Gargi rises before Yajnavalkya like a warrior with two arrows in hand, bringing two questions.

heals.why: she stands up a second time in a hall that expects her silence
she claims a warrior's stance for her questions

cultivates.why: she speaks as an equal to the champion of the debate
she comes prepared, with exactly two sharp questions

commentary.reading: Gargi, a knower of Brahman, takes the assembly's leave and challenges Yajnavalkya with two questions as hard to meet as a warrior's two arrows; they lead to the teaching of the imperishable.
commentary.source: Shankara on Brihadaranyaka 3.8.2

line_issue: The simile's warrior is a man of Kashi or Videha, and she rises before Yajnavalkya. Corrected: As a warrior strings his bow and stands with two sharp arrows, Gargi stood before Yajnavalkya with two questions.

claim: Rites and austerity without knowing the imperishable come to an end; one who dies without knowing it is pitiable.

heals.why: long effort and achievement are said to run out if the lasting thing was never known

cultivates.why: makes knowing the imperishable the one thing not to miss

needs: A hard verdict on a life; only for a seeker who asked the question.

commentary.reading: All works done without knowing the Akshara yield a finite result. He who departs without knowing it is a kripana, pitiable like a bought slave; he who departs knowing it is a brahmana.
commentary.source: Shankara on Brihadaranyaka 3.8.10

claim: Gargi tells the assembly that none of them will defeat Yajnavalkya and they should be glad to leave with a bow.

heals.why: the challenger herself names the other's superiority, aloud and without bitterness
conceding is done with grace and then silence

cultivates.why: honesty about who is better is shown as strength

commentary.reading: Having heard the answer on the imperishable, Gargi declares that no one will defeat him in the discussion of Brahman and falls silent.
commentary.source: Shankara on Brihadaranyaka 3.8.12

claim: A felled tree grows again from its root; from what root does a mortal grow again when cut down by death?

depicts.why: the question everyone carries about death, asked without an answer attached

needs: A challenge left unanswered by the assembly; the Upanishad itself answers with Brahman as knowledge and bliss. Alone it leaves a griever with nothing.

commentary.reading: Yajnavalkya asks the brahmins the root from which a dead man is reborn; they cannot answer, and the shruti gives it: Brahman, knowledge and bliss, the support of the giver and the knower.
commentary.source: Shankara on Brihadaranyaka 3.9.28

claim: As a caterpillar grasps the next blade before leaving the first, the self at death takes hold of another body.

heals.why: death is pictured as a crossing with no moment of falling into nothing
the one who died is shown as having moved on, already holding the next support

cultivates.why: the self is what passes over; the body is the blade left behind

needs: Assumes rebirth.

commentary.reading: The self, casting off this body and making it insensible, draws itself to another body shaped by its impressions, as the leech reaches the next straw. 'Avidyam gamayitva' means making the body unconscious, not giving up ignorance.
commentary.source: Shankara on Brihadaranyaka 4.4.3

claim: As a goldsmith makes a newer, finer form from gold, the self at death makes for itself a newer form.

heals.why: what is lost is a form; the gold is said to remain and be remade
the end of this body is described as a remaking

cultivates.why: the self is the gold, the body the shape it takes

needs: Assumes rebirth; the next verse ties the new form to one's deeds, so 'finer' is not promised to all.

commentary.reading: The self makes another body, of the manes, gandharvas, gods, Prajapati or other beings, according to its work and knowledge, as a goldsmith fashions a new form from the same gold.
commentary.source: Shankara on Brihadaranyaka 4.4.4

claim: One who knows the self as 'I am this' has nothing left to desire and no one for whose sake to suffer.

heals.why: fretting needs something still wanted for someone; the verse finds neither left
nothing is missing from what one is
with nothing to gain or lose for oneself, the fever goes

cultivates.why: the self is to be known directly as 'I am this'
fullness is one's own nature

commentary.reading: If a rare person knows the self as the supreme self, then, desiring what and for whose sake, would he suffer along with the body's afflictions? There is no second thing for him to want.
commentary.source: Shankara on Brihadaranyaka 4.4.12

claim: The knower's eternal greatness neither grows nor shrinks by action; calm and collected, he sees everything as the self.

heals.why: what one is at root is not made smaller by what one has done
a greatness that deeds can neither add to nor take from
nor is it enlarged by success

cultivates.why: sees the self in oneself and everything as the self
calm, restraint, patience and collectedness are the way in
worth that does not move with results

needs: 'Not stained by wrong action' describes the knower; it is no licence. Patience here is inner steadiness.

commentary.reading: The glory of the knower of Brahman is constant, neither increased by good work nor diminished by bad. Therefore, becoming calm, controlled, withdrawn from desires, forbearing and concentrated, he sees the self in his own self.
commentary.source: Shankara on Brihadaranyaka 4.4.23

line_issue: The line keeps only the five qualities and loses the verse's main statement. Corrected: What you are at root does not grow with good deeds or shrink with bad ones. Calm, restrained, patient and collected, one sees the self in oneself and in everything.

claim: That is whole and this is whole; when the whole is taken from the whole, the whole remains.

heals.why: nothing can be subtracted from what you are
the sense of lack is answered with fullness on both sides, there and here
what is whole has nothing to add

cultivates.why: fullness is where one starts from
a verse traditionally recited as a peace invocation
this, the self here, is as whole as that

commentary.reading: 'That' is the unconditioned Brahman, 'this' the same Brahman appearing with adjuncts as the world and the self; both are infinite. When the conditioned is known as the unconditioned, the infinite alone remains.
commentary.source: Shankara on Brihadaranyaka 5.1.1

claim: The first being feared when alone; seeing nothing other than himself, his fear left, for fear comes only from a second.

depicts.why: 'he was afraid; that is why one who is alone is afraid' gives fear to the very first being

heals.why: fear is traced to the sense of a second, and loosens when one looks for what exactly is other
being alone is turned from a threat into the fact that ends fear

cultivates.why: fearlessness is reached by looking, not by bravery
there is nothing other than the self to be afraid of

needs: For free-floating fear and dread. Not an answer to a concrete danger such as a diagnosis.

commentary.reading: Viraj feared as we do, from ignorance; fear left him through the knowledge that there is no second, since fear arises only from another.
commentary.source: Shankara on Brihadaranyaka 1.4.2

claim: The first being found no delight alone and longed for a second; so each person is like one half.

depicts.why: 'he found no delight; that is why one who is alone finds no delight'

heals.why: the wish for a companion is as old as the first being; it is no weakness

needs: Shankara reads the longing as desire still at work even in Prajapati, not as an ideal. Keep to the line; the following words on wife and progeny need their context.

commentary.reading: Being alone he had no delight, so he desired a mate and divided himself into husband and wife; this shows that even Prajapati is within the range of desire and ignorance.
commentary.source: Shankara on Brihadaranyaka 1.4.3

claim: By sheltering and feeding people, animals, birds and even ants, a householder becomes a world for them.

heals.why: ordinary providing is shown to matter to many beings

cultivates.why: feeding and housing others is what makes a home a world
the care reaches down to birds and ants
a household is seen as something many lives rest on

commentary.reading: The householder, through the five daily offerings to gods, sages, ancestors, people and animals, is a support for all beings, and so all beings wish him safe.
commentary.source: Shankara on Brihadaranyaka 1.4.16

claim: What is done with knowledge, faith and meditation becomes more powerful than the same act done without them.

heals.why: going through the motions is distinguished from the same act done with understanding

cultivates.why: faith is named as part of what gives an act its strength
the same work carries more when one knows why

commentary.reading: Both the knower of Om and the non-knower perform the rite, but what is done with knowledge of the syllable, faith and meditation is more potent in its result.
commentary.source: Shankara on Chandogya 1.1.10

claim: Austerity, giving, straightforwardness, non-harming and truthful speech are the gifts of the sacrifice that is a person's life.

cultivates.why: giving is one of the five offerings
non-harming is counted as an offering
discipline is the first of them

commentary.reading: In the meditation on a person's life as a sacrifice, these five virtues are its dakshina, since they strengthen dharma. Ghora Angirasa taught this to Krishna, son of Devaki.
commentary.source: Shankara on Chandogya 3.17.4

claim: Asked his lineage, Satyakama repeats his mother's words exactly and gives his name as Satyakama Jabala.

heals.why: he says the thing he might have hidden, in the same words he was given
the fear of being turned away does not make him invent a better story

cultivates.why: truth about oneself said to the person whose approval one needs

commentary.reading: The boy reports his mother's words without change; the teacher sees in this straightness the mark of a brahmin. On the mother's words see Shankara on 4.4.2: she was busy serving in her husband's house and never asked the gotra.
commentary.source: Shankara on Chandogya 4.4.4

claim: Though taught by others than men, Satyakama asks his teacher, since knowledge learned from a teacher best reaches its goal.

heals.why: already shining with what he knows, he still asks to be taught

cultivates.why: he trusts the teacher's word above his own attainment
knowing a great deal does not end the asking

commentary.reading: The bull, the fire, the swan and the diver-bird that taught him were deities; yet he asks his own teacher, for only knowledge learned from a teacher becomes best. The teacher taught the same, and nothing was left out.
commentary.source: Shankara on Chandogya 4.9.2-3

line_issue: 'Nature had taught him' is a modern gloss for 'others than men', whom Shankara takes as deities. Corrected: Though others than men had taught him, he still asked his teacher: knowledge learned from a teacher reaches furthest.

claim: The best among the senses is the one whose departure leaves the body worst off.

heals.why: the quarrel over who is best is settled by what happens when each one leaves
each sense that claimed first place turns out to be dispensable

cultivates.why: worth is measured by what depends on you, not by the claim

commentary.reading: Speech, sight, hearing and mind leave in turn and the body lives on; when the chief breath starts to leave, all are uprooted and admit it is the best.
commentary.source: Shankara on Chandogya 5.1.6-7

claim: A father admits to his humiliated son that he does not know the answers either, or he would have taught them.

heals.why: a renowned teacher says 'I do not know one of them' to his own son
the son's charge that his father held back is met with plain honesty

cultivates.why: honesty about one's limits inside the family
the father then goes to learn it himself

commentary.reading: Shvetaketu, unable to answer Pravahana Jaivali's five questions, reproaches his father; Gautama says he taught all he knew and goes himself to the king.
commentary.source: Shankara on Chandogya 5.3.5

claim: Offered wealth by the king, the father declines it and asks only for the teaching.

heals.why: wealth offered freely is set aside for something he wants more
an elder scholar asks a king to teach him

cultivates.why: he asks for the very words spoken to his son
'let the wealth stay with you'

commentary.reading: Gautama refuses the human wealth offered as a boon and asks for the knowledge of the five fires; the king is troubled because it had never before gone to a brahmin.
commentary.source: Shankara on Chandogya 5.3.6

claim: Knowing he could not answer everything, Uddalaka chose to direct the scholars to another teacher.

heals.why: the fear of being asked what one cannot answer is handled by saying who can
he does not bluff in front of great scholars

cultivates.why: knowing the edge of one's knowledge and acting on it

commentary.reading: Uddalaka judges that he cannot tell them the whole of the Vaishvanara self and takes them to King Ashvapati Kaikeya, who knows it.
commentary.source: Shankara on Chandogya 5.11.3

claim: A person should state the very purpose for which he has come.

heals.why: the hard conversation is reduced to one step: say why you are here

cultivates.why: directness, even when gifts and courtesy are offered instead
keeps to the reason one came

commentary.reading: The scholars decline the king's gifts: with whatever purpose a person comes, that alone he should speak of; they have come for the Vaishvanara self.
commentary.source: Shankara on Chandogya 5.11.6

claim: As one ember fed with straw blazes again, a mind reduced by fasting revives when fed, for mind is made of food.

heals.why: depletion is shown as a fire run low, which feeding brings back
not being able to think or remember is traced to an unfed body, not a failing mind

cultivates.why: one small ember is enough to rebuild from

commentary.reading: After fifteen days without food Shvetaketu cannot recall the Vedas; after eating he can. The experiment shows that the mind is nourished by food.
commentary.source: Shankara on Chandogya 6.7.5-6

claim: Rivers that merge in the sea become the sea and no longer know themselves as this or that river.

heals.why: the separate name each river carried is not what it finally is
every stream has the same sea as its source and end

cultivates.why: all beings come from one Being and return to it, mostly without knowing

needs: The point continues in 6.10.2: creatures coming from Being do not know it. Not a call to give up one's culture or identity.

commentary.reading: As rivers lose their names in the sea, so creatures who have come from Being do not know 'we have come from Being' and remain what they were; that Being is the self.
commentary.source: Shankara on Chandogya 6.10.1-2

claim: A dying man knows his relatives until speech merges in mind, mind in breath, breath in heat and heat in the highest.

depicts.why: relatives sit round the bed asking 'do you know me?'

heals.why: the moment he stopped knowing them is described as a merging into the highest, step by step

needs: Only for someone looking back on a death already past. Never while a relative is ill.

commentary.reading: The order of merging at death, speech into mind, mind into prana, prana into fire, fire into the supreme deity, is the same for all; the knower merges into Being without return.
commentary.source: Shankara on Chandogya 6.15.1

claim: One who covers himself with truth is not burned by the heated axe; one who covers himself with falsehood is burned.

cultivates.why: truth is pictured as a covering that protects

needs: An ancient ordeal used as an image for knowing or not knowing Being. Read plainly it implies that whoever suffers was guilty.

commentary.reading: The one whose resort is the true, Being, is not burned and is released, that is, not reborn; the one whose resort is the false is burned and killed, that is, returns to birth.
commentary.source: Shankara on Chandogya 6.16.1-2

line_issue: The translation's 'is punished' softens 'is killed'. The verse should be held back; if used: The one who stood in truth took the heated axe and was not burned.

claim: One acts only on finding happiness in it; no one acts without finding happiness.

heals.why: not acting is traced to finding no joy in the thing, which is information and not a character flaw
explains why work that has lost its joy stops moving

cultivates.why: ask what happiness the action is for

commentary.reading: A person engages in effort only when he expects happiness; that happiness, rightly understood, is the infinite taught next.
commentary.source: Shankara on Chandogya 7.22.1

claim: What people call greatness, cattle, gold, land and houses, is not greatness, since each rests on something else.

heals.why: possessions are refused the name of greatness
what others have is dependent greatness at best
more holdings do not add up to standing on one's own

cultivates.why: real greatness rests on nothing outside itself

needs: The Sanskrit list includes servants and wives among possessions; keep to the line.

commentary.reading: The infinite rests in its own greatness, or not even in greatness, for worldly greatness means one thing depending on another; Sanatkumara denies that sense.
commentary.source: Shankara on Chandogya 7.24.2

claim: Virochana taught the asuras that the body alone is the self to be served, and that this wins both worlds.

cultivates.why: shows how a half-heard teaching becomes a creed of the body

needs: This is the mistaken doctrine in the story. Never standalone.

commentary.reading: Virochana, satisfied with the reflection in water, took the body to be the self and taught that; the Upanishad calls this the doctrine of the asuras.
commentary.source: Shankara on Chandogya 8.8.4

claim: If the self is the body, it is blind, lame and destroyed when the body is; Indra sees no good in that.

depicts.why: Indra stops halfway home because the answer he was given does not hold
he sees that a self that is only the body ends with it

cultivates.why: he tests the teaching against what it implies
he turns back to ask again

needs: The list of blindness and injury is hard on someone ill or disabled.

commentary.reading: Indra, being of better understanding, sees the defect in taking the body's reflection as the self and returns to Prajapati, fuel in hand.
commentary.source: Shankara on Chandogya 8.9.1

claim: Prajapati confirms Indra's doubt and asks him to stay another thirty-two years to be taught further.

heals.why: the teacher's first words to the doubt are 'so it is'

cultivates.why: he stays, again and again, a hundred and one years in all
the doubt is taken back to the teacher, not away from him

commentary.reading: Prajapati accepts the objection and promises to explain the same self further once Indra has lived another term as a student, which purifies him for it.
commentary.source: Shankara on Chandogya 8.9.3

claim: The mortal body is the dwelling of the deathless, bodiless self, whom pleasure and pain do not touch.

heals.why: what death holds is the dwelling, not the one who dwells
the swing of pleasure and pain belongs to identifying with the body

cultivates.why: you live in the body; you are not it

commentary.reading: The body is seized by death; it is the seat of the immortal, bodiless self. Embodiedness is the false identification with the body; when that goes through knowledge, pleasure and pain do not touch one.
commentary.source: Shankara on Chandogya 8.12.1

line_issue: The line keeps only the negative half. Corrected: This body is mortal; it is the home of a self that is not. While you take yourself to be the body, pleasure and pain keep their grip. They do not touch what you are.

claim: One who studies, lives as a householder, keeps learning, raises virtuous children, steadies the senses and harms no being reaches Brahman's world.

heals.why: a household life lived well is given the highest end

cultivates.why: a whole life of steady, ordinary practice
harming no living being
the senses gathered into the self

commentary.reading: The closing verse shows the householder's path: study, home, continued recitation, virtuous sons and pupils, withdrawal of the senses, non-injury except as scripture ordains. So living he reaches Brahmaloka and does not return.
commentary.source: Shankara on Chandogya 8.15.1

claim: The face of truth is covered by a golden vessel; the seer asks the Sun to uncover it.

depicts.why: someone who holds to truth asks for the bright covering to be lifted

heals.why: what hides the real is said to be something golden and attractive

cultivates.why: seeing is asked for, not seized
the prayer trusts that there is a face behind the lid

commentary.reading: The prayer of the dying meditator to the Sun: Brahman called Satya, in the solar orb, is hidden by a shining disc; remove it for me whose dharma is truth.
commentary.source: Shankara on Isha 15

claim: A prayer to Agni to lead us by the good path and keep crooked wrongdoing away.

heals.why: before a decision, one asks to be led by the straight road
asks for one's crookedness to be removed, without self-punishment

cultivates.why: the one who knows all our ways is asked to lead
trust that there is a good path

commentary.reading: The departing worshipper asks Agni to lead him by the good path, the northern way, to the enjoyment of his works' fruit, and to remove deceitful sin.
commentary.source: Shankara on Isha 18

claim: For one who sees all beings as the one self, there is no delusion and no sorrow.

heals.why: grief rests on a sense of separation that this seeing removes
confusion has no footing where everything is known as one self
nothing is finally apart from oneself

cultivates.why: all beings have become the self for the one who knows

needs: Describes the knower. Never say it to a griever as 'there is no reason to grieve'.

commentary.reading: Sorrow and delusion come to one who does not know the cause, desire and action; for the seer of the one pure self they are impossible, ignorance being uprooted.
commentary.source: Shankara on Isha 7

line_issue: 'The same life' softens 'the self'. Corrected: For one who sees all beings as the one self, what confusion and what grief can remain?

claim: Yama grants that Nachiketa's father will recognise him, lose his anger and sleep in peace.

heals.why: a father's anger is shown ending, and his sleep returning

cultivates.why: the son's first wish is for his father's peace
the boy asks nothing against the father who sent him away

needs: Nachiketa's own choice inside his story. Not a rule that the hurt child must make peace first.

commentary.reading: The first boon: the father will be as affectionate as before, free of anger, and sleep happily on seeing his son released from Death.
commentary.source: Shankara on Katha 1.1.11

claim: Pressed three times by his son, the father says in anger, 'I give you to Death.'

depicts.why: a parent's worst sentence, said in a flash of temper

needs: Only inside the Nachiketa story, where the father regrets it at once.

commentary.reading: Nachiketa, full of faith, sees the worn-out cows being given and asks to whom he himself will be given; the father, irritated, speaks in anger.
commentary.source: Shankara on Katha 1.1.4

claim: Nachiketa reflects that he has never been last among sons or pupils and wonders what purpose of Yama he will serve.

cultivates.why: he walks toward Death thinking it through, without panic
he knows his own conduct was not at fault

commentary.reading: Among many sons or disciples I rank first or middling, never last; yet father spoke so. What work of Yama's will he accomplish through me today? Others read: many have died before me and many will after.
commentary.source: Shankara on Katha 1.1.5

line_issue: 'What can Death really do with me' turns a puzzled question into bravado. Closer: Among many I walk first, among many in the middle. What work can Death have for me today?

claim: Mortals ripen and fall like grain and like grain are born again, as those before and after us show.

heals.why: dying is set inside a cycle as ordinary as a harvest

cultivates.why: in a life this brief, keeping one's word matters more than keeping one's comfort

needs: In the story Nachiketa says this so that his father keeps his word. Assumes rebirth.

commentary.reading: Consider how your forefathers behaved and how the good behave now: none broke his word. Man decays and is born again like corn; what is gained by falsehood in so transient a world?
commentary.source: Shankara on Katha 1.1.6

claim: Knowing the self as bodiless within bodies, steady among the unsteady, great and all-pervading, the wise one does not grieve.

heals.why: what is loved and what loves has a part that change does not reach
in every upheaval something stays where it was
uncertainty is about the unsteady things; the verse points to the steady one

cultivates.why: the self is the stable one among all that shifts
steadiness borrowed from what is steady

commentary.reading: The self is bodiless by nature, present in impermanent bodies of gods, men and others, great and all-pervading; knowing 'I am this', the wise do not grieve.
commentary.source: Shankara on Katha 1.2.22

claim: The self is not reached by teaching, intellect or much learning; it reveals itself to the one it chooses.

heals.why: cleverness and scholarship are denied the last step
not being learned is no bar

cultivates.why: the last step is given, not taken
what counts is wanting the self itself

commentary.reading: Shankara: the self is attained by that very self which the seeker longs for; to one who seeks it alone it reveals its nature. Ramanuja and Gita Press read: it is gained by the one whom the Lord chooses, by grace.
commentary.source: Shankara on Katha 1.2.23; Gita Press

claim: One who has not ceased from wrong conduct and whose mind is not calm and collected cannot reach the self by intelligence.

heals.why: says plainly that insight will not come while conduct is left as it is

cultivates.why: a quiet, collected mind is the precondition
cleverness is not the same as readiness

needs: Reads as blame to someone already ashamed of a habit.

commentary.reading: Only one who has turned from prohibited acts, quieted the senses, gathered the mind and is not anxious even for the fruit of that calm attains the self through knowledge.
commentary.source: Shankara on Katha 1.2.24

claim: Without understanding and a steady mind the senses bolt like wild horses; with them the senses obey like good horses.

heals.why: the bolting is a matter of reins not held, which can be learned
impulse is a horse, strong and trainable
an outburst is the team running without the driver

cultivates.why: understanding is the driver
a mind always held steady

commentary.reading: When the intellect lacks discrimination and the mind is unyoked, the senses are uncontrollable like vicious horses; with a discerning intellect and yoked mind they are controllable.
commentary.source: Shankara on Katha 1.3.5-6

claim: The immature follow outward desires into death's wide net; the wise do not seek the lasting among things that pass.

heals.why: shows where the outward chase ends
the lasting is not among what is being collected

cultivates.why: tell the lasting from the passing
stop asking permanence of impermanent things

commentary.reading: Those of little understanding pursue external objects and fall into the snare of death, ignorance, desire and action; the discerning, knowing the sure immortality of the inner self, pray for nothing here.
commentary.source: Shankara on Katha 2.1.2

claim: As the sun is not stained by faults the eyes see, the one inner self is not stained by the world's sorrow.

heals.why: the light by which a fault is seen is not itself faulty
there is something in you that sorrow lights up but does not mark
what others say and see does not reach it

cultivates.why: the inner self illumines everything and is touched by none of it
one can see pain fully and not be made of it

commentary.reading: People superimpose sorrow on the self through ignorance, as a snake on a rope; the one self within all is outside that sorrow, as the sun helps every eye and is untouched by the impurity seen.
commentary.source: Shankara on Katha 2.2.11

claim: Sun, moon, stars, lightning and fire do not light that; everything shines after it and by its light.

heals.why: whatever is seen at all is evidence of the light it is seen by

cultivates.why: the awareness by which everything is known is prior to every other light
a verse of plain wonder
the mind rests on the source of all brightness

commentary.reading: The sun and the rest cannot illumine Brahman, the self; they shine only by its light, as hot iron burns by fire's heat. Its being self-luminous is known from all else shining.
commentary.source: Shankara on Katha 2.2.15

claim: When all the knots of the heart are cut here in this life, the mortal becomes immortal; that is the whole teaching.

heals.why: the knots are the ties of 'I am this, this is mine'; they can be cut while living
a knotted heart can be loosened here, not in some other life

cultivates.why: freedom is placed in this life
the whole teaching comes down to untying
