commentary.reading: The knots are the convictions born of ignorance, 'I am this body, this wealth is mine, I am happy or unhappy', with the desires rooted in them. When knowledge destroys them the mortal becomes immortal, here.
commentary.source: Shankara on Katha 2.3.15

claim: One should not seek to know speech, action or pleasure and pain, but the knower of them.

heals.why: attention is turned from the contents of worry to the one aware of them
the stream of sensations has one steady knower

cultivates.why: know the one who knows pleasure and pain
separates experience from the experiencer

commentary.reading: Indra directs the inquiry from each object and function to its knower, the conscious self (prajnatman), on which all are fixed like spokes on a hub.
commentary.source: Kaushitaki 3.8 plain sense; chapter read as Brahman in Shankara on Brahma Sutra 1.1.28-31

line_issue: 'Don't chase' is not in the text. Corrected: Do not study your pleasure and pain. Know the one who knows them.

claim: A dying father places his faculties, joys and sorrows in his son, and the son receives each.

heals.why: what a father was is shown passing into the child, piece by piece and with consent

cultivates.why: the child says 'I take it' to everything given

needs: For someone looking back on a parent's death. Never while the parent is ill.

commentary.reading: The rite of transmission (sampradana): the father about to die hands over speech, breath, sight, deeds, joys and sorrows to the son, who accepts each.
commentary.source: Kaushitaki 2.15 plain sense; no bhashya checked

claim: Trees, animals and birds also live; the one who truly lives is the one whose mind lives by reflection.

heals.why: mere going on is distinguished from living with thought

cultivates.why: reflection is what makes a life human
asks what one's days are actually spent on

needs: Can sound like a verdict that an unreflective life is worthless.

commentary.reading: Part of Nidagha's lament on the emptiness of mere living. The Yoga Vasishtha parallel reads 'mananena na jivati', whose mind does not live on by thinking, which gives a different sense; this record's reading is kept but is uncertain.
commentary.source: Maha Upanishad, Ribhu and Nidagha dialogue; plain sense. The verse parallels the Yoga Vasishtha; no classical bhashya checked (Vairagya Prakarana)

claim: Scripture burdens the undiscerning, knowledge the passionate, the mind the restless, and the body one who does not know the self.

depicts.why: 'the mind is a burden to the one who is not at peace'
even one's learning and one's own body are felt as weight

commentary.reading: Nidagha's lament: without discernment, calm and self-knowledge, the very things meant to help become loads to carry.
commentary.source: Maha Upanishad, Ribhu and Nidagha dialogue; plain sense. The verse parallels the Yoga Vasishtha; no classical bhashya checked (Vairagya Prakarana)

claim: Whatever good quality I take up, craving cuts through it, as a mouse gnaws through a string.

depicts.why: first person: every resolve I make, craving chews through
the discouragement of watching one's own good intentions cut

commentary.reading: Nidagha confesses that craving destroys each virtue he tries to hold.
commentary.source: Maha Upanishad, Ribhu and Nidagha dialogue; plain sense. The verse parallels the Yoga Vasishtha; no classical bhashya checked (Vairagya Prakarana)

claim: Craving is a restless monkey: it reaches where it cannot go, strives even when satisfied, and never stays in one place.

depicts.why: wanting that keeps going even after it has been fed
never long in one place

commentary.reading: Nidagha's picture of craving as a fickle monkey that is never satisfied.
commentary.source: Maha Upanishad, Ribhu and Nidagha dialogue; plain sense. The verse parallels the Yoga Vasishtha; no classical bhashya checked (Vairagya Prakarana)

claim: The good do not wilt in adversity, want nothing beyond what is at hand and delight in the path of the good.

heals.why: offers a picture of not collapsing when things go wrong

cultivates.why: staying open in the dark, like the golden lotus at night
wanting nothing beyond what the moment gives

needs: Praise of the steady can read as a reproach to someone who has wilted. Use as an aspiration.

commentary.reading: In praise of those who follow the way of the wise: adversity does not make them droop.
commentary.source: Maha Upanishad, Ribhu and Nidagha dialogue; plain sense. The verse parallels the Yoga Vasishtha; no classical bhashya checked

claim: All beings, harsh and gentle alike, come to trust a calm person as they would a mother.

heals.why: gives a reason, in a conflict, to be the calm one

cultivates.why: calm is shown as what makes others feel safe
trust grows around the one who does not react

commentary.reading: In praise of shama: every creature, fierce or mild, confides in the tranquil person as in a mother.
commentary.source: Maha Upanishad, Ribhu and Nidagha dialogue; plain sense. The verse parallels the Yoga Vasishtha; no classical bhashya checked (Mumukshu Prakarana)

claim: The content person does not long for what has not come, enjoys what has come and stays even in gain and loss.

heals.why: attention returns from what others got to what has actually come to you
the not-yet is let go

cultivates.why: a working definition one can test oneself against
even with what comes

needs: Not an answer to being passed over unfairly.

commentary.reading: Definition of santosha, the third doorkeeper: giving up desire for the unattained and being even-minded with the attained.
commentary.source: Maha Upanishad, Ribhu and Nidagha dialogue; plain sense. The verse parallels the Yoga Vasishtha; no classical bhashya checked (Mumukshu Prakarana)

claim: 'I am Brahman' frees; the word 'mine' binds a creature and 'not mine' releases it.

heals.why: the grip is located in one word, 'mine'
ownership is shown as the bond itself

cultivates.why: 'not mine' as a way of holding things
'I am Brahman' is named the cause of freedom

needs: About clinging, not about ceasing to care for one's family.

commentary.reading: Bondage and release turn on two words, mama and nirmama; the conviction 'I am Brahman' is the cause of liberation.
commentary.source: Maha Upanishad, Ribhu and Nidagha dialogue; plain sense. The verse parallels the Yoga Vasishtha; no classical bhashya checked

claim: Non-clinging alone is freedom; clinging is sorrow.

heals.why: the pain is put in the holding on
resentment is also a way of holding on

cultivates.why: freedom defined as an open hand

needs: Not clinging is not the same as not caring. Not for bereavement or for someone wronged.

commentary.reading: Anastha, placing no reliance on objects, is itself nirvana; taking up reliance on them is suffering.
commentary.source: Maha Upanishad, Ribhu and Nidagha dialogue; plain sense. The verse parallels the Yoga Vasishtha; no classical bhashya checked

claim: However brave, learned, well born or great, a person is bound by craving as a lion by a chain.

heals.why: being caught by craving happens to the strongest; it is no proof of being weak
no rank or learning puts anyone beyond it

commentary.reading: Craving binds even the wise and the great.
commentary.source: Maha Upanishad, Ribhu and Nidagha dialogue; plain sense. The verse parallels the Yoga Vasishtha; no classical bhashya checked

claim: Neither neglect nor luxury moved Shuka's mind; he stayed even, clear, silent and glad, like the full moon.

heals.why: luxury offered freely does not pull him

cultivates.why: the same under being ignored and under being pampered
a mountain in a light breeze

commentary.reading: Janaka tests Vyasa's son Shuka, first by keeping him waiting at the gate and then with pleasures; finding him unmoved, he confirms that Shuka already knows what is to be known.
commentary.source: Maha Upanishad 2.26-27; the story is also told in the Yoga Vasishtha and the Mahabharata; plain sense

claim: The mark of the wise is not longing for pleasures yet to come and enjoying those that have come.

heals.why: the future result is not waited on
no pining for what has not arrived

cultivates.why: enjoy what is here, without effort or show

commentary.reading: Natural, unforced absence of desire for future enjoyments, with full use of those present, is the mark of the pandita.
commentary.source: Maha Upanishad, Ribhu and Nidagha dialogue; plain sense. The verse parallels the Yoga Vasishtha; no classical bhashya checked

claim: A king asks what use enjoyments are and begs to be lifted out like a frog from a dark well.

depicts.why: he has had everything and asks what use any of it is
'I am like a frog in a dark well'
'you are my way, you are my way'

commentary.reading: King Brihadratha, having set his son on the throne and practised austerity, sees the body and the world as passing and takes refuge in the sage Shakayanya, who then teaches him the self.
commentary.source: Maitri Upanishad 1.7; plain sense

claim: Everything here is seen to perish, like gnats, mosquitoes, grass and trees that arise and are destroyed.

depicts.why: a king looks at everything and sees only that it ends

needs: Only as the opening of Brihadratha's story, followed by the sage's answer.

commentary.reading: Brihadratha's survey of impermanence: even great kings, oceans and gods pass away.
commentary.source: Maitri Upanishad 1.4; plain sense

claim: Seeing non-difference is knowledge, an objectless mind is meditation, shedding the mind's dirt is bathing, and sense-restraint is purity.

heals.why: one who cannot keep the outer observances is shown their inner meaning

cultivates.why: each ritual is traced to what it is for
meditation defined as a mind at rest from objects

commentary.reading: Shiva gives the inner sense of knowledge, meditation, bathing and purity for the renunciant.
commentary.source: Maitreya Upanishad 2.2; plain sense

claim: Shaunaka asks what it is that, once known, makes all this known.

depicts.why: a man with a great household comes with one question

commentary.reading: Shaunaka, a great householder, approaches Angiras as scripture requires and asks for the one cause by knowing which everything is known.
commentary.source: Shankara on Mundaka 1.1.3

claim: Those who live in ignorance yet think themselves wise go round and round, like the blind led by the blind.

heals.why: self-certainty is shown as the thing that keeps one circling

cultivates.why: check whether one's guide can see

needs: Aimed at those satisfied with ritual and status. As a line to a struggling reader it is an insult.

commentary.reading: Those immersed in ritual works, thinking themselves wise and learned, are battered by old age and disease and wander like blind men led by a blind man. The same verse stands at Katha 1.2.5.
commentary.source: Shankara on Mundaka 1.2.8

claim: Om is the bow, the self the arrow and Brahman the target; hit it undistracted and become one with it.

heals.why: gives the mind one line of aim
'by one who is not heedless'

cultivates.why: the self is sent into Brahman like an arrow into its mark
meditation on Om as the method

commentary.reading: Om is the bow by which the self, as arrow, enters the imperishable; one free of the heedlessness of desire for objects, with a concentrated mind, should hit the mark and become one with it.
commentary.source: Shankara on Mundaka 2.2.4

line_issue: The line removes Om, the self and Brahman and leaves a tip on concentration. Corrected: Om is the bow, the self the arrow, Brahman the target. Aim undistracted and, like the arrow, become one with it.

claim: When the highest is seen, the knot of the heart is cut, all doubts end and one's deeds wear away.

heals.why: doubt ends by seeing, not by one more argument
what one has done loses its hold in that seeing
the heart's knot is cut

cultivates.why: seeing that which is both cause and effect
the heart unknotted

commentary.reading: The knot is the mass of desires and ignorance lodged in the intellect; on seeing the self that is both high as cause and low as effect, it breaks, doubts end and actions not yet begun to bear fruit are destroyed.
commentary.source: Shankara on Mundaka 2.2.8

claim: On the same tree the person sits sunk, grieving in helplessness; seeing the other, the Lord, he becomes free of sorrow.

depicts.why: 'sunk, he grieves'
the word is helplessness: grieving because one feels powerless
bewildered

heals.why: grief lifts on noticing who else is on the same branch
the greatness one lacks is found in one's closest companion

cultivates.why: turn and see the one who watches
the other bird is the Lord, and the looking is a kind of leaning

commentary.reading: The individual, sunk in the body under the weight of ignorance and desire, grieves from impotence, thinking 'I am good for nothing'. When through practice he sees the Lord as his own self and this glory as his, he is freed from grief.
commentary.source: Shankara on Mundaka 3.1.2

claim: The knower of the one life in all beings does not out-talk others; delighting in the self, he stays active.

heals.why: joy is shown as available inside an active life

cultivates.why: play and delight in the self
one life shines through every being
active, not withdrawn

commentary.reading: Knowing the Lord as the prana of all, the wise one has no urge to surpass others in speech. He sports and delights in the self; his 'activity' is knowledge, meditation and dispassion.
commentary.source: Shankara on Mundaka 3.1.4

claim: One who dwells on desires is born wherever they lead; for one fulfilled in the self all desires dissolve here.

heals.why: brooding on wants is what multiplies them
wanting ends in fullness, not in getting

cultivates.why: the one whose desire is fulfilled in the self
wholeness within is where desires go quiet

commentary.reading: He who longs for objects, thinking of their merits, is born amid those very objects. For one whose desires are fulfilled by knowing the self, all desires vanish even here.
commentary.source: Shankara on Mundaka 3.2.2

claim: The self is not won by the weak, the careless or by aimless austerity, but by the wise who strive.

heals.why: carelessness is named as what loses it

cultivates.why: strength is required, and can be had
the one who strives arrives
steady, aimed effort

needs: 'Not for the weak' wounds someone who feels weak.

commentary.reading: Strength is that which comes of steady devotion to the self; pramada is heedlessness from attachment; 'tapas without its mark' Shankara takes as knowledge without renunciation.
commentary.source: Shankara on Mundaka 3.2.4

claim: As rivers enter the sea and give up name and form, the knower, freed from name and form, reaches the supreme Person.

heals.why: name and form are what is given up; nothing real is lost
the end of separateness is an arrival

cultivates.why: the knower's identity is the sea, not the river's name

needs: Speaks of the knower's liberation, not of an ordinary death. Do not offer it as a statement about someone who has died or is ill.

commentary.reading: As rivers lose their distinct names and forms on reaching the sea, the enlightened one, freed from name and form made by ignorance, attains the self-effulgent Person higher than the unmanifest.
commentary.source: Shankara on Mundaka 3.2.8

claim: Heaven is the company of the good; hell is keeping company with the unreal and with people absorbed in it.

heals.why: what one keeps company with is what one's days become

cultivates.why: choose company as one would choose a world to live in

commentary.reading: In the catechism, svarga is defined as association with the good and naraka as association with worldly people sunk in unreal objects.
commentary.source: Niralamba Upanishad 17; plain sense

claim: The stainless world of Brahman belongs to those in whom there is no crookedness, falsehood or deceit.

heals.why: when the crooked option tempts, the verse names what straightness keeps

cultivates.why: integrity as one's whole qualification

commentary.reading: The pure Brahmaloka is for those free of the crookedness, untruth and deceit that worldly dealings breed.
commentary.source: Shankara on Prashna 1.16

claim: When the life-breath rose to leave, all the senses had to rise with it, like bees following their queen.

heals.why: the senses that boasted find they cannot even stay without the breath
rank is settled by dependence, not by claims

commentary.reading: The senses claim to uphold the body; prana, to show them, begins to leave and all are dragged along, as bees follow the king bee. They then praise prana.
commentary.source: Shankara on Prashna 2.4

claim: The sage asks the seekers to live one more year in discipline and faith and then ask their questions.

heals.why: even the teacher says 'if we know'

cultivates.why: a year of preparation before the question
they stay
'ask whatever you wish'

commentary.reading: Though already disciplined, the six are to dwell a further year with austerity, continence and faith; the teacher's 'if we know' shows his freedom from conceit.
commentary.source: Shankara on Prashna 1.2

claim: Seekers ask whence we are born, by what we live, where we rest and who governs our joy and sorrow.

depicts.why: the oldest questions, asked together and without embarrassment

commentary.reading: The knowers of Brahman deliberate together on the cause of the world and of our pleasures and pains.
commentary.source: Shvetashvatara 1.1; plain sense following the bhashya attributed to Shankara

claim: As oil is in sesame and butter in curd, the self is found within by one who seeks with truth and discipline.

heals.why: what is sought is already inside, as surely as oil is in the seed
nothing has to be brought in from outside

cultivates.why: the self is hidden in oneself and can be drawn out
truthfulness and discipline are the pressing and churning

commentary.reading: The self is grasped in one's own self by truth and austerity, as oil is got by pressing and butter by churning.
commentary.source: Shvetashvatara 1.15; plain sense following the bhashya attributed to Shankara

claim: That self-made reality is the very essence; on gaining that essence a person becomes joyful.

heals.why: the flatness of things is answered by pointing to what gives anything its taste

cultivates.why: joy is traced to one source, tasted in every joy
every moment of gladness is a taste of it

commentary.reading: Brahman, called the self-made because it made itself, is rasa, the source of joy; only by getting that does anyone become happy, as even desireless sages are seen to be.
commentary.source: Shankara on Taittiriya 2.7

line_issue: The translation's 'well made' misses 'sukrita' as the self-made. Line is acceptable; closer: It is the very essence. Whoever finds that essence becomes joyful.

claim: One who knows the bliss of Brahman, from which words and mind turn back, fears nothing at all.

heals.why: fear needs something that can be taken away; the joy described is out of reach of anything
the mind is told there is a place it need not, and cannot, work out

cultivates.why: fearlessness comes from knowing a joy that is one's own
the bliss of Brahman is the self's own nature

commentary.reading: Words and mind, which make everything else known, fall back from the non-dual bliss; the knower of it as his own self has no cause of fear anywhere, since fear comes from a second.
commentary.source: Shankara on Taittiriya 2.9

claim: Varuna tells Bhrigu to seek that from which beings are born, by which they live and into which they return.

cultivates.why: the father gives a definition to search by, not a conclusion
Bhrigu goes away and works on it

commentary.reading: Varuna gives the doors to Brahman, food, breath, eye, ear, mind and speech, and its mark as the source, support and end of beings; Bhrigu is to discover it by tapas.
commentary.source: Shankara on Taittiriya 3.1

claim: Brahman is to be sought through tapas, concentrated reflection, which is itself Brahman.

cultivates.why: each incomplete answer is met with 'go back and reflect again'
the search itself is honoured as the thing sought

commentary.reading: Tapas is the best means: here the concentration of the outer and inner organs. Varuna calls it Brahman because it is the means to knowing Brahman, and repeats it each time.
commentary.source: Shankara on Taittiriya 3.2

claim: One should not speak ill of food; that is a vow.

cultivates.why: respect for what keeps the body and breath going, kept as a daily vow

commentary.reading: Since Brahman was approached through food, the knower keeps the vow of not disparaging food; body and breath are food and eater to each other.
commentary.source: Shankara on Taittiriya 3.7

claim: One should turn no one away from one's dwelling; that is a vow, so one should gather plenty of food.

cultivates.why: the door stays open as a matter of vow
whoever comes for shelter is received

needs: Hospitality, not a duty to house someone who mistreats you.

commentary.reading: The vow of not refusing anyone who comes for lodging; since a guest must be fed, one should earn much food by whatever proper means.
commentary.source: Shankara on Taittiriya 3.10. The Sanskrit field carries stray section headings

claim: Right conduct, truth, austerity and self-control are each to be practised together with study and teaching.

cultivates.why: learning runs alongside every other duty, never replaced by them
a short list to live by

commentary.reading: Study and teaching are repeated with each duty to show they must be kept up with care along with all the others.
commentary.source: Shankara on Taittiriya 1.9

claim: Do not be careless about truth, dharma, your welfare, your prosperity, or study and teaching.

heals.why: looking after one's own wellbeing is listed as a duty beside truth and dharma
five things not to drift from

cultivates.why: keeps welfare and prosperity inside a dharmic life

needs: The verse also says not to cut the family line; the line rightly leaves that out for general use.

commentary.reading: Kushala is action for one's own protection, bhuti action for prosperity; neither is to be neglected, along with truth, dharma and study.
commentary.source: Shankara on Taittiriya 1.11.1

claim: Only blameless actions are to be done; of the teachers' conduct, only the good is to be followed.

heals.why: honouring elders and declining to copy their faults are shown as compatible
the teacher himself grants that not all his conduct deserves following

cultivates.why: sort an elder's example into what to keep and what to leave
one's own conscience is given standing

commentary.reading: Even among the acts of teachers, only those not opposed to scripture are to be practised, not the others.
commentary.source: Shankara on Taittiriya 1.11.2

claim: Seeking freedom, I take refuge in the God who gave Brahma the Vedas and lights up the understanding of the self.

depicts.why: first person: longing to be free, I go for refuge

cultivates.why: inquiry ends in leaning on the one who lights the mind
understanding itself is received as a gift

commentary.reading: The seeker of liberation takes refuge in the Lord who reveals knowledge of the self in the intellect.
commentary.source: Shvetashvatara; plain sense following the bhashya attributed to Shankara and Gita Press

claim: The Lord who shines through all the senses and rules all is the refuge and friend of all.

heals.why: the highest is called everyone's friend
no one is outside 'the refuge of all'
the one who rules everything is on your side

cultivates.why: power and friendliness are said of the same Lord
a refuge that is already open to all

commentary.reading: The Lord is without organs yet illumines the work of all organs; he is master, refuge and well-wisher of all. Some recensions read 'the great refuge' in place of 'friend'.
commentary.source: Shvetashvatara; plain sense following the bhashya attributed to Shankara and Gita Press

claim: The self is hidden in every creature's heart; one free of desire sees it by grace and is freed from sorrow.

heals.why: sorrow lifts in seeing what is lodged in one's own heart
the greatest thing there is lives in the smallest creature

cultivates.why: the self is hidden in the heart
the seeing is received by grace

commentary.reading: The self dwells in the cave of the heart; one without desire for results sees that Lord and his greatness through the Creator's grace and becomes free of grief. Katha 1.2.20 has the same verse.
commentary.source: Shvetashvatara; plain sense following the bhashya attributed to Shankara and Gita Press

claim: A frightened person takes refuge in Rudra as the Unborn and asks to be protected always by his kind face.

depicts.why: the seer calls himself afraid and does not hide it
he comes to the Unborn for shelter

heals.why: fear is given somewhere to go

cultivates.why: asking for protection is itself the practice

needs: A prayer, not a promise about outcomes.

commentary.reading: One afraid of birth, death and sorrow resorts to Rudra, the unborn, and prays for protection by his benign face.
commentary.source: Shvetashvatara; plain sense following the bhashya attributed to Shankara and Gita Press

claim: A prayer that Rudra look upon us with his auspicious, unfrightening, most peaceful form.

heals.why: asks the power one fears to turn its gentle side

cultivates.why: the form invoked is the most peaceful one
a request to be looked upon kindly

commentary.reading: From the Shatarudriya: Rudra's benign form, not terrible and revealing no evil, is asked to shine on the worshippers.
commentary.source: Shvetashvatara; plain sense following the bhashya attributed to Shankara and Gita Press

claim: Knowing the one Lord in whom all this gathers and dissolves, the giver of blessings, one reaches lasting peace.

heals.why: everything that worries the mind is said to rest in one who is kind

cultivates.why: peace is tied to knowing who holds the whole
the Lord is named giver of blessings

commentary.reading: By realising the one Lord who presides over every source and in whom the world comes together and separates, one attains supreme peace.
commentary.source: Shvetashvatara; plain sense following the bhashya attributed to Shankara and Gita Press

claim: Knowing the auspicious One, subtle, in the midst of confusion, creator and sole encompasser of all, one reaches lasting peace.

heals.why: the chaos is not denied; something kind is placed in the middle of it
in the thick of confusion there is one who holds the whole

cultivates.why: peace that does not wait for the chaos to end
the world is held, 'encompassed', by one

commentary.reading: Shiva, subtler than the subtle, stands in the midst of the tangle of the world as its maker and sole pervader; knowing him one attains peace.
commentary.source: Shvetashvatara; plain sense following the bhashya attributed to Shankara and Gita Press

claim: Knowing the guardian of the world hidden in all beings, one cuts the nooses of death.

heals.why: the world is said to have a guardian through time

cultivates.why: the protector is hidden in every being
death's nooses are cut by knowledge

needs: 'Loosens death's hold' means freedom through knowledge, not recovery from illness.

commentary.reading: He protects the world at the proper time and is hidden in all beings; knowing him, one cuts the bonds of death, that is, of ignorance and its results.
commentary.source: Shvetashvatara; plain sense following the bhashya attributed to Shankara and Gita Press

claim: One God, hidden in all beings, is their inner self, the overseer of action, the witness, pure awareness, beyond qualities.

heals.why: no one is ever unaccompanied; the same one dwells in each
the inner self of every being is the one God
there is a witness to what one does, quiet and unshaken

cultivates.why: the innermost self is the witness, awareness itself
the same one is hidden in the other person

commentary.reading: The one self-luminous God is concealed in all beings as their inner self, presides over all actions, and is the witness, the conscious one, alone and free of the gunas.
commentary.source: Shvetashvatara; plain sense following the bhashya attributed to Shankara and Gita Press

claim: A prayer that Rudra not harm our children, our lives or our people in his anger.

depicts.why: a parent's fear for the little ones, said straight to God

heals.why: fear for a loved one is given words and somewhere to be placed

cultivates.why: 'we call on you always'

needs: A prayer of fear, no promise of an outcome; never in place of medical help.

commentary.reading: A Rig Vedic mantra (1.114.8) also in the Shatarudriya, asking Rudra not to injure children, life, cattle or heroes.
commentary.source: Shvetashvatara; plain sense following the bhashya attributed to Shankara and Gita Press

claim: I take refuge in the goddess Durga, fire-coloured and blazing with tapas, who destroys darkness.

heals.why: refuge is taken in a power that burns
she is asked to clear the darkness

cultivates.why: 'I take refuge'
the refuge is fierce, and lends that fierceness

commentary.reading: The Durga Sukta verse (Taittiriya Aranyaka 10.1): refuge in Durga, radiant like fire, who carries her devotees across difficulties.
commentary.source: Devi Upanishad (Devi Atharvashirsha); plain sense as recited with the Durga Saptashati, Gita Press

claim: Salutations to the Goddess; may the Mother protect us on every side.

heals.why: protection is asked on every side, as a child asks
the one addressed is 'Mother'

cultivates.why: a child's direct request

commentary.reading: The gods salute the Goddess as Mother and ask her protection; she is then identified with the Vasus, Rudras and Adityas.
commentary.source: Devi Upanishad (Devi Atharvashirsha); plain sense as recited with the Durga Saptashati, Gita Press

claim: I bow always to the Goddess who removes affliction, grants enjoyment and liberation, and is the kind refuge.

heals.why: she is named the one who takes away burning pain

cultivates.why: she is called sharanya, fit to be taken refuge in
she gives both the good of this life and freedom

commentary.reading: Praise of the Goddess as remover of the three kinds of affliction and giver of both bhukti and mukti.
commentary.source: Devi Upanishad (Devi Atharvashirsha); plain sense as recited with the Durga Saptashati, Gita Press

claim: I bow to the Goddess who destroys great fear, calms great hardship and is compassion in form.

heals.why: she is addressed as the destroyer of great fear

cultivates.why: courage borrowed from the one bowed to
the bow itself

commentary.reading: Closing salutation to the Goddess as destroyer of great fear and of great difficulty, whose form is great compassion.
commentary.source: Devi Upanishad (Devi Atharvashirsha); plain sense as recited with the Durga Saptashati, Gita Press

claim: The Goddess is called Durga because nothing is higher than her and because she rescues from hardship.

heals.why: the name itself means the one who brings you through the hard pass
a hard place is something one is carried across

cultivates.why: trust in being brought through
strength to keep walking the hard stretch

needs: Strength to face hardship, not a guarantee it disappears.

commentary.reading: The etymology of the name: she saves from durga, difficulty, and there is none beyond her.
commentary.source: Devi Upanishad (Devi Atharvashirsha); plain sense as recited with the Durga Saptashati, Gita Press

claim: Afraid of worldly existence, I bow to Durga, destroyer of wrongdoing, who carries us across its ocean.

depicts.why: 'frightened by this life, I bow'

heals.why: the frightened person has someone to bow to who ferries across

cultivates.why: fear turned into a bow

commentary.reading: The devotee, afraid of samsara, salutes Durga who destroys evil conduct and takes one across the ocean of worldly existence.
commentary.source: Devi Upanishad (Devi Atharvashirsha); plain sense as recited with the Durga Saptashati, Gita Press

claim: The Goddess is the power of the self and the great knowledge; whoever knows her so crosses beyond grief.

heals.why: grief is something one can cross, with her as the knowledge that carries

cultivates.why: she is the power of one's own self
knowing her is named the crossing

needs: A direction, not a deadline for grieving.

commentary.reading: She is atma-shakti, the enchantress of the world and Shri Mahavidya; the knower of this crosses sorrow.
commentary.source: Devi Upanishad (Devi Atharvashirsha); plain sense as recited with the Durga Saptashati, Gita Press

claim: By a trace of Mahadeva's compassion I am unshaken; I am pure consciousness, I am Shiva.

heals.why: what I am is said to be Shiva, by his own kindness

cultivates.why: the realisation is received as compassion and thanked for
'I am a mass of knowing, I am Shiva'
'what could be beyond this?'

commentary.reading: The opening declaration: through the Lord's grace the devotee is achyuta, unfallen, and knows himself as consciousness and as Shiva.
commentary.source: Skanda Upanishad 1; plain sense, no bhashya checked

line_issue: The line drops the verse's centre, 'I am Shiva'. Corrected: Mahadeva, by a trace of your compassion I stand unshaken. I am pure knowing, I am Shiva. What could be more than this?

claim: With dispassion as oil and devotion as wick, the lamp of knowledge rises by itself in the darkness of delusion.

heals.why: the darkness is called hollow; a small lamp is enough for it

cultivates.why: letting go is the fuel
devotion is the wick
the light then rises of itself

commentary.reading: Markandeya's image of how knowledge of Shiva as the teacher dawns: dispassion, devotion and awakening prepare the lamp, and knowledge shines of itself.
commentary.source: Dakshinamurti Upanishad; plain sense, no bhashya checked

claim: I bow to Vishnu, peaceful in form, support of the universe, who removes the fear of worldly existence.

heals.why: he is addressed as the remover of the fear of this life

cultivates.why: the first word is 'peaceful in form', and the verse is a picture to rest the mind on
the bow

commentary.reading: The traditional dhyana verse of Vishnu, recited before the Vishnu Sahasranama; it is appended to printed editions and is not part of the Upanishad's own text.
commentary.source: Traditional dhyana shloka; plain sense

claim: May my mind, the far-travelling light of lights in waking and in sleep, be of auspicious resolve.

depicts.why: a mind that travels far whether one is awake or asleep

heals.why: the wandering is not fought; a wish is laid on where it goes

cultivates.why: 'may my mind be of good resolve' as a nightly and morning refrain
a prayer traditionally said before sleep

commentary.reading: The mind is divine, the one light of the senses, going far in waking and returning in sleep; the seer prays that it hold auspicious intentions.
commentary.source: Shukla Yajurveda (Vajasaneyi Samhita) 34.1, following Uvata and Mahidhara in outline

claim: May my mind, which leads people as a good charioteer leads horses, be of auspicious resolve.

heals.why: the swiftest thing in us is asked to drive well
the reins are prayed over before the horses bolt

cultivates.why: the driver of one's life is asked to intend well
the mind is 'set in the heart'

commentary.reading: As a skilled charioteer directs horses with reins, the mind directs people; seated in the heart, unageing and swiftest, may it be of auspicious resolve.
commentary.source: Shukla Yajurveda (Vajasaneyi Samhita) 34.6, following Uvata and Mahidhara in outline

claim: Real character shows in a person's most common actions, not in great performances.

heals.why: one big success proves little about who one is

cultivates.why: the small daily acts are where character is built
look at the ordinary, in oneself and others

commentary.reading: Greatness is being the same always; occasions make even small men heroic for a moment.
commentary.source: Swami Vivekananda, Karma-Yoga, ch. 1 (Complete Works); verbatim passage, read in its own context

claim: Misery, poverty and blows have taught great characters more than happiness, wealth and praise.

heals.why: a setback is placed in the history of every strong character
failure is read as schooling, not as verdict

cultivates.why: blows are said to bring out inner fire
hard times are given a use

needs: Never to someone wronged or bereaved, to whom it says the hurt was good for them.

commentary.reading: Pain and pleasure are both teachers of the soul, and pain has usually taught more.
commentary.source: Swami Vivekananda, Karma-Yoga, ch. 1 (Complete Works); verbatim passage, read in its own context

claim: We are responsible for what we are and have the power to make ourselves whatever we wish to be.

heals.why: the power to remake oneself is said to be already in hand
nothing outside has to change first

cultivates.why: what I wish to be is mine to build
self-reliance without apology

needs: 'Responsible for what we are' wounds someone who was harmed by others or by illness.

commentary.reading: From the law of karma: if our present is our own making, so is our future.
commentary.source: Swami Vivekananda, Karma-Yoga, ch. 1 (Complete Works); verbatim passage, read in its own context

claim: To help someone or do good work, do not think about their attitude to you or what the result will be.

heals.why: the result is taken off the table while working
no watching for how the helped person responds

cultivates.why: work complete in itself

commentary.reading: His gloss on Gita 2.47: the right is to work, the fruits are to be left alone.
commentary.source: Swami Vivekananda, Karma-Yoga, ch. 1 (Complete Works); verbatim passage, read in its own context

claim: The ideal person finds intense activity in silence and the silence of the desert in intense activity.

heals.why: the noise can stay outside while the work goes on
calm is described as portable

cultivates.why: a cave carried into the street
rest and action held together

commentary.reading: The ideal of Karma-Yoga: calm as in a cave while working intensely in the city.
commentary.source: Swami Vivekananda, Karma-Yoga, ch. 1 (Complete Works); verbatim passage, read in its own context

claim: Our first duty is not to hate ourselves; faith in oneself comes first and then faith in God.

heals.why: self-hatred is named as the thing to stop first, before any improvement
faith in oneself is called a duty

cultivates.why: trust in oneself is made the first step to trust in God
self-respect as the base

commentary.reading: A warning against ideals so high that they breed self-hatred; one advances only from self-respect.
commentary.source: Swami Vivekananda, Karma-Yoga, ch. 2 (Complete Works); verbatim passage, read in its own context

claim: Each person should be judged by the standard of their own ideal, as an apple tree by the apple standard.

heals.why: the other person's yardstick is the wrong one for you
not being an oak is no failure in an apple tree

cultivates.why: take up your own ideal
rest in your own kind of fruit

commentary.reading: Each is great in his own place; no one ideal fits all.
commentary.source: Swami Vivekananda, Karma-Yoga, ch. 2 (Complete Works); verbatim passage, read in its own context

claim: To keep doing good without caring for anyone's approval is the hardest thing and the highest sacrifice.

heals.why: the wait for thanks is named and let go

cultivates.why: doing right with no audience
help given without a claim on gratitude

needs: Not to someone whose credit was taken; it tells them to stop minding.

commentary.reading: On the householder's duty: anyone is brave when praised; the test is good done unseen.
commentary.source: Swami Vivekananda, Karma-Yoga, ch. 2 (Complete Works); verbatim passage, read in its own context

claim: Fear is weakness; one must do one's duty without noticing the world's sneers and ridicule.

heals.why: the fear here is of mockery, and it is given no vote

cultivates.why: go on regardless
one's duty outweighs the crowd

needs: The line alone is safe. The passage's 'fear is a sign of weakness' shames an anxious reader.

commentary.reading: The Vedas' one word is fearlessness; fear is called a sign of weakness.
commentary.source: Swami Vivekananda, Karma-Yoga, ch. 2 (Complete Works); verbatim passage, read in its own context

claim: Good thoughts and good works leave impressions whose sum forces a person toward good even in spite of himself.

heals.why: habit is shown to work in one's favour too
each small good act counts toward a tide

cultivates.why: start laying down the other kind of impression
repetition does the work

commentary.reading: Character is the sum of samskaras; good ones accumulate just as bad ones do.
commentary.source: Swami Vivekananda, Karma-Yoga, ch. 3 (Complete Works); verbatim passage, read in its own context

claim: One should work incessantly, as a master and not as a slave.

heals.why: the drag in work is traced to working under compulsion of wants
work without being owned by it

cultivates.why: stand as master of one's work
freedom inside effort

needs: About inner attachment, not about one's employer.

commentary.reading: Slave's work is work done from selfish attachment; the master works from freedom and love.
commentary.source: Swami Vivekananda, Karma-Yoga, ch. 3 (Complete Works); verbatim passage, read in its own context

claim: Love brings only bliss; what brings a painful reaction is something else mistaken for love.

heals.why: possessiveness is separated from love
